threads.summary_md: Gad opens his deathbed testament by retracing the quarrel Genesis records: Joseph, feeding the flock with his brethren and the sons of Bilhah, carries to their father the report that they were slaying the best of the flock — and Gad is wroth with him until the day he is sold. It ain't new — the testament only confesses from the inside the very evil report and grudge Moses set down.

threads.title: The spirit of hatred — would not hear or see his brother
threads.summary_md: Gad confesses that the spirit of hatred was in him, so that he wished not to hear of Joseph with the ears nor see him with the eyes. The apostle John names the same darkness: he that hateth his brother walketh in darkness and his eyes are blinded. It ain't new — the testament's confession is the very blindness John warns the children against.

threads.title: Hatred unto murder — hated for his dreams
threads.summary_md: Gad confesses that he often wished to kill Joseph, hating him from the heart and yet the more for his dreams. Genesis records the dreams that drew the brethren's hatred — *And his brethren said to him, Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us? And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words* (Genesis 37:8) — and the apostle John names what such hatred truly is — *Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him* (1 John 3:15). It ain't new — Gad's confession is the very murder in the heart that John warns against.

threads.title: Judah sold him to the Ishmaelites — yet God delivered him
threads.summary_md: Gad recalls that Judah sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites through covetousness, yet the God of their fathers delivered him out of their hands, that they should not work great lawlessness in Israel. Genesis records both the selling and that God meant the evil for good. It ain't new — the testament reads Joseph's deliverance just as Joseph himself read it to his brethren.

threads.title: Hatred blindeth the soul — work all the law of the Most High
threads.summary_md: Gad exhorts his children to work righteousness and all the law of the Most High, and to go not astray through the spirit of hatred — for the hater dispraiseth truth and envieth him that prospers, since hatred blindeth his soul. The Torah forbids the hatred outright, and Solomon names what it breeds. It ain't new — Gad presses no new law, only the love-of-neighbour Moses commanded against the strife hatred stirs.

threads.title: Hatred will not hear the commandment concerning loving one's neighbour
threads.summary_md: Gad warns that hatred worketh lawlessness even against the Lord, for it will not hear His commandments concerning the loving of one's neighbour. He names the precise Torah word it refuses — the command to love thy neighbour as thyself. It ain't new — the lawlessness of hatred is measured against the very statute Moses gave.

threads.title: Hatred worketh unto death, love unto salvation
threads.summary_md: Gad sets the two spirits side by side: the spirit of hatred worketh together with Satan unto men's death, but the spirit of love worketh together with the law of God in long-suffering unto the salvation of men. The apostle John draws the same line — we have passed from death unto life because we love the brethren. It ain't new — Gad's two spirits are John's two states, death and life, told beforehand.

threads.title: Humility destroyeth envy — and Gad's own liver judged
threads.summary_md: Gad teaches that humility destroyeth envy, and confesses that because his liver was set mercilessly against Joseph, in his liver too he suffered mercilessly — by what things a man transgresseth, by the same is he punished. Solomon names envy as the very rottenness of the bones. It ain't new — Gad's body bore in itself the proverb Israel already knew.

threads.title: Drive forth hatred which is of the devil — cleave to the love of God
threads.summary_md: Gad describes hatred mating with lying, kindling wrath and stirring up war, and bids his children drive it forth and cleave to the love of God. The apostle Paul gives the same charge — put away all bitterness, wrath, anger, and evil speaking. It ain't new — Gad's plea to cast out hatred is Paul's word to the saints, spoken long before.

threads.title: Love one another from the heart — put away hatred
threads.summary_md: The heart of Gad's testament: love one another from the heart, and put away hatred from your hearts — in deed, in word, and in the inclination of the soul. He had spoken peaceably to Joseph before his father while the spirit of hatred darkened his mind; now he commands the love Torah commands. It ain't new — love thy neighbour as thyself is Moses' own word, and the message John says was heard from the beginning.

threads.title: If a man sin against thee — rebuke, and if he repent, forgive him
threads.summary_md: Gad lays down the rule: if a man sin against thee, speak peaceably to him and hold no guile; if he repent and confess, forgive him. The Messiah gives word for word the same order — go and tell him his fault, and forgive thy brother seventy times seven. It ain't new — the Lord's forgiveness teaching and Gad's deathbed counsel are one path of rebuke-and-pardon.

threads.title: Even the shameless — forgive him from the heart, and leave to God the avenging
threads.summary_md: Gad reaches the hardest word: even if a man be shameless and persist in his wrong-doing, even so forgive him from the heart, and leave to God the avenging. Paul says forgive even as God forgave you; the Lord says forgive from your hearts; and vengeance belongs to God alone. It ain't new — heart-forgiveness that leaves vengeance to God is Moses, the Messiah, and the apostle in one voice.

threads.title: If a man prosper more than you, be not vexed but pray for him
threads.summary_md: Gad turns from hatred to its twin, envy: if a man prospereth more than you, be not vexed but pray for him; if he be exalted, be not envious. David's psalm gives the same medicine — fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be envious against the workers of iniquity. It ain't new — Gad's cure for envy is the song Israel already sang.

threads.title: Though a man grow rich by evil means as Esau — wait for the end of the Lord
threads.summary_md: Gad counsels that though a man become rich by evil means, even as Esau, be not jealous but wait for the end of the Lord — for the unrepentant is reserved for eternal punishment, while the poor man free from envy is blessed beyond all men. The psalm shows the same end: the wicked spreading like a green bay tree, yet passing away and found no more. It ain't new — the testament's patience is the psalmist's confidence in how the wicked end.

threads.title: Honour Judah and Levi — from them the Lord shall raise up salvation
threads.summary_md: Gad's closing charge before he falls asleep: tell your children to honour Judah and Levi, for from them shall the Lord raise up salvation to Israel. This is the testaments' joined hope — the sceptre of Judah and the priesthood of Levi meeting in one Anointed. It ain't new — Balaam saw the Star out of Jacob, and Zechariah saw the Branch who is priest upon his throne, the counsel of peace between the two.

threads.title: Asher's two ways — good and evil set before the sons of men
threads.summary_md: Asher opens his deathbed testament with the doctrine of the two ways: two ways God has given to the sons of men, two inclinations in the breast, the way of good and the way of evil, and the soul must cleave to one. This is the oldest framework in Scripture — Moses sets life and good over against death and evil and bids Israel choose; the Messiah narrows it to the strait gate and the broad way. It ain't new — the two ways the patriarch teaches are the two ways Deuteronomy and the Gospel set before every man.

threads.title: The two inclinations — repentance, or rule by Beliar
threads.summary_md: Asher describes the two inclinations warring in the breast: the soul that takes pleasure in the good repents straightway when it sins and uproots the evil, but the soul that inclines to the evil is ruled by Beliar, who perverts even its good to evil. The prophets and apostles know this same contest — sin conceived bringing forth death, and the heart drawn away by its own lust. It ain't new — the two inclinations Asher names are the lust that wars within and the new heart that turns and repents.

threads.title: The hare — half clean yet unclean, by the tables of the commandments
threads.summary_md: Asher's catalogue of the two-faced man ends in a striking figure: the man who sins greatly yet keeps some commandments, who fasts yet does evil, is like the hare — half clean, but in very deed unclean — for, he says, God in the tables of the commandments hath thus declared. The patriarch reaches straight for Torah's law of clean and unclean, where the hare is named unclean because it answers one mark of cleanness but not the other. It ain't new — Asher reads the two-faced soul off the very dietary law Moses wrote, and treats those commandments as standing and binding.

threads.title: He defraudeth his neighbour, yet pitieth the poor — the whole is evil
threads.summary_md: Among the two-faced men Asher exposes is the one who defrauds his neighbour, swears falsely, sets the law of the Lord at nought — and yet pities the poor, as though the one good covers the many evils. Torah forbids the very fraud and false swearing he indulges, and the Lord who commands the law is the One he provokes. It ain't new — Asher measures the double-faced almsgiver by the law of the Lord that he sets at nought.

threads.title: Wear not two faces — the double-minded who serve not God
threads.summary_md: Here is Asher's keystone charge: wear not two faces of goodness and of wickedness, but cleave to goodness only, for the double-faced serve not God but their own lusts, to please Beliar. This is the same single-heartedness the Messiah demands — no man can serve two masters — and the double-minded man James says is unstable in all his ways and must purify his heart. It ain't new — the two-faced man Asher warns against is the double-minded man Scripture calls to one Master and one heart.

threads.title: Men of single face — just before God, like the clean stag and hind
threads.summary_md: Asher turns to the good men of single face: though the double-faced think they sin, they are just before God; they are like stags and hinds, which seem wild and unclean but are altogether clean, because they walk in zeal for the Lord and abstain from what God hateth and forbiddeth by His commandments. The single face is the single eye that fills the whole body with light, and the clean creature is read straight off Torah's law of clean and unclean. It ain't new — the single-faced man Asher commends keeps the very commandments of God that mark clean from unclean.

threads.title: Asher's own walk — singleness of face, searching out the commandments
threads.summary_md: Asher closes his teaching on the two by witnessing to his own life: he proved all these things, wandered not from the truth of the Lord, and searched out the commandments of the Most High, walking with singleness of face unto good. The man who keeps one face is the doer who looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues in it, blessed in his deed. It ain't new — Asher's singleness of face is a life spent searching out and keeping the commandments, the doer's path the apostle commends.

threads.title: Keep the law of the Lord — the double-faced sin twofold
threads.summary_md: Asher exhorts his children to keep the commandments and the law of the Lord, following truth with singleness of face, for the double-faced are guilty of a twofold sin — both doing evil and delighting in those who do it. The apostle marks the same double guilt of those who not only do such things but have pleasure in them that do them, and James calls the wavering, double-minded man unstable. It ain't new — Asher's charge to keep the law with one face is the apostolic call away from the twofold sin of the divided heart.

threads.title: The latter end of a man — the angel of peace and eternal life
threads.summary_md: Asher tells how the latter ends of men show their righteousness: the troubled soul departs to torment by the evil spirit it served, but the peaceful soul meets the angel of peace, who leads it into eternal life. The two ways run all the way to the two ends Moses set before Israel — life and death — and to the eternal life laid up for them that love the Lord. It ain't new — the two destinies Asher sees at death are the life and death Deuteronomy set before every soul, and the crown of life the apostle promises.

threads.title: Scattered to the four corners — set at nought as useless water
threads.summary_md: Asher's closing prophecy is the two-house word: Israel shall sin, be delivered to its enemies, its land made desolate and holy places destroyed, and be scattered to the four corners of the earth, set at nought in the dispersion as useless water — scattered like Gad and Dan, no longer knowing land, tribe, or tongue. This is precisely the curse Moses spoke for forsaking the law. It ain't new — the scattering Asher foresees is the dispersion Deuteronomy and Leviticus pronounced for despising the commandments.

threads.title: The Lord shall gather you in faith through His tender mercy
threads.summary_md: After the scattering, Asher's hope: the Lord will gather you together in faith through His tender mercy, for the sake of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This is the second word of the two-house promise — Moses foretold not only the scattering but the return and gathering when Israel turns, and the prophets see the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah gathered from the four corners and made one nation again. It ain't new — the gathering Asher promises is the return Deuteronomy and the prophets bound up in God's mercy to the fathers.

threads.title: The Most High shall visit, break the head of the dragon, and save Israel and the Gentiles
threads.summary_md: At the centre of Asher's hope the Most High Himself shall visit the earth, break the head of the dragon in the water, and save Israel and all the Gentiles. Some later hands gloss this as God walking as man; the genuine root is the prophets' word that the Lord shall slay the dragon in the sea, and that His salvation reaches both Israel and the nations through the root of Jesse. It ain't new — the Most High visiting to crush the serpent and save both Israel and the Gentiles is the prophets' own hope, fulfilled in the Anointed One.

threads.title: Joseph's confession — hated by his brethren, but the Lord was with him
threads.summary_md: Joseph opens his deathbed testament with the litany of his life: his brethren hated him and would have slain him, they let him into a pit and sold him into slavery, yet at every turn Yahuah delivered, nourished, comforted, and exalted him. It ain't new — this is the very arc Moses set down in Genesis and the Psalmist sang of the man sold for a servant whom the word of Yahuah tried.

threads.title: He struggled against a shameless woman, and God delivered him
threads.summary_md: Pharaoh's captain entrusts his house to Joseph, and at once Joseph struggles against the shameless woman who urges him to transgress — the temptation Genesis records, here owned as a fire from which the God of Israel delivered him. Cast into prison, beaten, mocked, he still finds mercy with the keeper. It ain't new — Moses already told both the refusal and the favour Joseph found in the prison.

threads.title: Threatened day by day, he remembered his father's words and prayed
threads.summary_md: The Egyptian woman threatens, flatters, and offers him lordship of her house, but Joseph remembers his father's words, weeps and prays, fasts, drinks no wine, and gives his food to the poor and sick. Genesis says she spake to Joseph day by day, and he hearkened not — the testament fills in the disciplines by which he held fast. It ain't new — youthful lusts are fled by the pure heart that seeks Yahuah early.

threads.title: The Lord takes no pleasure in adultery, but in the pure heart
threads.summary_md: The woman flatters Joseph as a holy man, then offers to leave her idols and walk in the law of his Lord if only he will lie with her. Joseph answers that Yahuah wills no uncleanness, takes no pleasure in adultery, but delights in those who approach Him with a pure heart and undefiled lips. It ain't new — the commandment is a lamp that keeps a man from the flattering tongue of the strange woman.

threads.title: The wickedness of the ungodly has no power over those who worship with chastity
threads.summary_md: The woman sends food laced with enchantments, but the God of Joseph's fathers reveals her wickedness by His angel; Joseph eats it openly, calling on the God of his fathers and the angel of Abraham, to prove that no ungodly device prevails against those who worship God with chastity. It ain't new — God is faithful in temptation and makes the way of escape for them that fear Him in darkness and in bonds.

threads.title: He left his garment behind and fled away naked
threads.summary_md: She lays hold of his garments and forcibly drags him; Joseph leaves the garment behind and flees away naked, and on the strength of that garment she falsely accuses him, and he is scourged and sent to Pharaoh's prison. This is the very scene of Genesis 39 — the caught garment, the flight, the false charge, the prison. It ain't new — Moses already set down the garment left in her hand.

threads.title: God loves him who in a den of darkness combines fasting with chastity
threads.summary_md: Even from prison she keeps soliciting, offering freedom for consent, but not in thought does Joseph incline to her; God loves the man who in a den of darkness joins fasting with chastity more than the man who in kings' chambers joins luxury with licence, and Yahuah guards Joseph from all her devices. It ain't new — youthful lust is fled by following righteousness with a pure heart, and the tried man receives the crown of life.

threads.title: Sold, he refrained from telling he was the son of Jacob
threads.summary_md: Joseph turns from the chastity narrative to its fruit: how great things patience and prayer with fasting work, so that the Most High dwells with the chaste and exalts him. He marks his own restraint — though loved above his brethren and being sold by them, he did not raise himself against them with evil intent, but out of respect refused to tell the Ishmaelites that he was the son of Jacob. It ain't new — this is the Joseph who would say, ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good.

threads.title: He confessed himself a slave that he might not put his brethren to shame
threads.summary_md: Joseph exhorts his sons to fear God and honour their brethren, for every one who does the law of Yahuah is loved by Him. He recalls that when the Ishmaelites asked whether he was a slave, he answered that he was a home-born slave, that he might not put his brethren to shame — choosing his own dishonour over their exposure. It ain't new — to love thy neighbour as thyself, and to bear long with a brother's fault, is the whole of the law.

threads.title: His bowels melted, yet he restrained himself for his brethren's sake
threads.summary_md: The Ishmaelites tell Joseph that his father mourns him in sackcloth; his bowels are dissolved and his heart melts, and he longs to weep — yet he restrains himself, still saying "I am a slave," that he should not put his brethren to shame. This is the very tenderness Genesis records when Joseph at last could not refrain himself. It ain't new — the Messiah-type silently bears his own grief rather than expose those who wronged him.

threads.title: He returned their money, upbraided them not, and comforted them
threads.summary_md: Joseph charges his sons to love one another and with long-suffering hide one another's faults, for God delights in the unity of brethren. When his brethren came into Egypt he returned their money, upbraided them not, and comforted them; after Jacob's death he loved them yet more, counting their children his, their suffering his, and exalting not himself but being among them as one of the least. It ain't new — this is Joseph who comforted them and spake kindly, the Messiah-type who forgives and saves.

threads.title: If any seek to do you evil, do well unto him and pray for him
threads.summary_md: Joseph's closing charge: walk in the commandments of Yahuah, and if any one seeks to do you evil, do well unto him and pray for him, and you shall be redeemed of Yahuah from all evil. He points to himself — out of humility and long-suffering God gave him a wife, gold, beauty, and length of days. It ain't new — to love your enemies and overcome evil with good is the Messiah's own word, the fruit of Joseph's whole long-suffering life.

threads.title: The vision — from a virgin a lamb is born, and a lion at his hand
threads.summary_md: Joseph's deathbed vision: from Judah a virgin in a linen garment, and from her a spotless lamb; at his left hand as it were a lion; all the beasts rush against him, and the lamb overcomes and treads them under foot. The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world and the Lion of the tribe of Judah are seen together centuries before the cross. It ain't new — Moses, Isaiah, and the prophets had already drawn the virgin, the lamb, and the lion of Judah.

threads.title: Ye shall carry up my bones with you out of Egypt
threads.summary_md: Joseph dies at a good old age with a charge: God will visit Israel and bring them into the land He promised the fathers, and they shall carry up his bones with them. So it came to pass — at the Exodus the children of Israel took the bones of Joseph and buried him among his fathers. It ain't new — Moses kept this oath and carried up the bones, and Joshua laid them in the ground of the inheritance.

threads.title: Rachel's barren years, her prayer, and the son of her sorrow
threads.summary_md: Benjamin opens by retelling Moses exactly: Rachel barren after Joseph, her long-withheld womb opened in answer to prayer, and her death in giving him birth on the way to Ephrath. Genesis even keeps the two names — Ben-oni, the son of her sorrow, and Benjamin, the name his father gave. It ain't new — the testament only confesses on the deathbed the very birth the Torah had already written.

threads.title: The bloodied coat and the brother sold to the Ishmaelites
threads.summary_md: Joseph tells Benjamin what the brothers reported to Jacob — that they dipped the coat in blood — and what they truly did: stripped him of it and gave him to the Ishmaelites. The testament simply gives Joseph's voice to the deeds Moses records. It ain't new — the dabbled coat and the selling are the Torah's own account of the wrong Joseph would later forgive.

threads.title: Love the Lord God and keep His commandments, love thy neighbour
threads.summary_md: Benjamin's whole charge stands on the two great commands: love the Lord God of heaven and earth and keep His commandments, and love thy neighbour. The man who does both — the example is Joseph — cannot be ruled by the spirit of Beliar, for he is shielded by the fear of God. It ain't new — this is Moses and the Prophets in two clauses, the very pair the Messiah named the whole law and the prophets hang upon.

threads.title: Joseph besought his father to pray that their sin be not imputed
threads.summary_md: The mark of the good man, says Benjamin, is that Joseph asked Jacob to pray that the Lord would not impute to his brethren the evil they did him — the man who was sold interceding for those who sold him. Genesis sets the pattern: Joseph weeps, comforts, and forgives, naming the very providence that turned their evil to good. It ain't new — the mercy that returns good for evil and prays for the offender is the Torah's love-of-neighbour carried to its height.

threads.title: A blameless one delivered up for lawless men, for the salvation of all
threads.summary_md: Jacob's blessing over Joseph reaches past Joseph: a prophecy that a blameless one shall be delivered up for lawless men, a sinless one die for the ungodly, for the salvation of the Gentiles and of Yashar'el (Israel), to destroy Beliar. Joseph is the good man who was sold and forgave, and the prophecy points beyond him to the Branch from Levi and Yahudah (Judah), the Anointed delivered up and raised. It ain't new — *He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth* (Isaiah 53:7) — the lamb led to the slaughter in Isaiah is the one Joseph's life points to.

threads.title: The good man hath not a dark eye, for he showeth mercy to all
threads.summary_md: The good man, Benjamin says, hath not a dark eye but shows mercy to all men, even sinners; on the poor he has mercy, on the weak compassion. The Messiah's own teaching turns on the same image — the single eye that fills the whole body with light — and on the mercy that obtains mercy. It ain't new — the bright eye and the merciful heart are the Torah's love of neighbour seen plainly.

threads.title: By doing good he overcometh evil, and envieth not
threads.summary_md: Though men devise evil against him, the good man overcomes evil by doing good, and he envies none — not the glorified, not the rich, not the valiant. Paul writes the same charge to the Romans almost word for word: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good. It ain't new — the apostle's rule of the renewed mind is the deathbed wisdom of Benjamin.

threads.title: The holy man is merciful to his reviler; humbled a little, glorified after
threads.summary_md: The good mind disarms even the violent: the holy man is merciful to his reviler and holds his peace, and the betrayed righteous man prays — humbled for a little, but soon appearing far more glorious, as Joseph was. Joseph in the pit and prison, then over Egypt, is the very pattern; and the Messiah, reviled and silent, then ascending in glory, is its fulfilment. It ain't new — the abasement-before-exaltation of the righteous runs from Joseph through the Servant of Isaiah.

threads.title: One disposition, uncorrupt and pure — no double tongue, no double sight
threads.summary_md: The good mind, Benjamin teaches, has not two tongues of blessing and cursing, nor double sight nor double hearing; it has one disposition, pure toward all men, for the Lord is its portion. James names the same single-heartedness against the double-minded man, and the Messiah against the tongue that says more than yea and nay. It ain't new — the undivided heart whose portion is the Lord is the longing of the Psalms.

threads.title: Cain delivered to sevenfold vengeance — the wages of brother-hatred
threads.summary_md: Benjamin warns that the sword of Beliar is the mother of seven evils, and grounds the warning in Cain, delivered to sevenfold vengeance and Lamech to seventy times seven — and all who are like Cain in envy and hatred of brethren fall under the same judgment. Genesis sets the sevenfold and seventy-sevenfold; John names plainly what brother-hatred is. It ain't new — that the hater of his brother is a murderer is written from the first blood spilled in the field.

threads.title: The pure mind looketh not after a woman to fornication
threads.summary_md: He that has a pure mind in love, Benjamin says, looks not after a woman with a view to fornication, for the Spirit of God rests on him; as the sun is undefiled though it shine on mire, so the pure mind cleanses and is not defiled. The Messiah set the same standard at the root, in the heart that looks. It ain't new — purity of heart, not merely of deed, is the law's own measure, and the pure in heart shall see God.

threads.title: From the words of Enoch the righteous — the fornication of Sodom
threads.summary_md: Benjamin names his source: the words of Enoch the righteous, foreseeing that his sons will commit the fornication of Sodom and renew wanton deeds with women. Enoch's own book records the fornication and the defiling with women that filled the earth with corruption, and Jude couples Sodom's strange flesh with the angels who left their estate. It ain't new — Benjamin reads the latter-day apostasy out of Enoch, the very witness the apostle Jude would later quote by name.

threads.title: The last temple more glorious, the twelve tribes and all Gentiles gathered
threads.summary_md: Yet the temple of God shall be in their portion, and the last temple more glorious than the first; there the twelve tribes shall be gathered, and all the Gentiles, until the Most High sends forth His salvation. Haggai promised the latter house greater than the former, and Isaiah saw all nations flowing to the mountain of the Lord's house. It ain't new — the two-house ingathering of all twelve tribes with the nations is the prophets' settled hope.

threads.title: The Lord lifted up upon a tree, and the veil of the temple rent
threads.summary_md: The prophecy then darkens: the Lord shall be treated with outrage and lifted up upon a tree, and the veil of the temple rent, and the Spirit pass to the Gentiles as fire poured forth. The Anointed of Levi and Judah is the one lifted up; Moses already wrote that the hanged one bears a curse, and the Gospel records the veil torn from top to bottom at the very hour. It ain't new — the tree, the curse borne, and the rent veil are written in the Torah and fulfilled in the Branch.

threads.title: The Spirit to the Gentiles, and He shall ascend from Hades into heaven
threads.summary_md: The Spirit of God shall pass to the Gentiles as fire poured forth, and He shall ascend from Hades and pass from earth into heaven — lowly upon earth, glorious in heaven. Paul reads the same descent and ascent into the lower parts and up far above the heavens, and Peter tells how He preached to the spirits in prison. It ain't new — the One who descends and ascends, pouring the Spirit on the nations, is the hope the prophets and apostles share.

threads.title: Keep the law and commandments, the fathers' inheritance, till salvation comes
threads.summary_md: Benjamin's dying charge is the fathers' charge: keep the law of the Lord and His commandments, the inheritance Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob handed down — until the Lord reveal His salvation to all Gentiles. Moses set the same commandment as Israel's very life, and Isaiah promised the Servant given for a light to the Gentiles. It ain't new — the keeping of the commandments and the salvation reaching the nations are one inheritance from the fathers.

threads.title: Enoch, Noah, and the fathers rise — each one over his tribe
threads.summary_md: Then, Benjamin says, you shall see Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rising on the right hand in gladness, and we also rise, each one over his tribe, worshipping the King of heaven. The Messiah declared God the God of the living, not the dead — the fathers live to Him — and promised the twelve to sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes. It ain't new — the rising of the fathers and the twelve set over the tribes is the resurrection hope the Gospel confirms.

threads.title: All men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame
threads.summary_md: The resurrection is universal: all men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame, and the Lord shall judge Israel first for their unrighteousness. Daniel saw the sleepers awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame; the Messiah named the resurrection of life and the resurrection of damnation; John saw the dead, small and great, judged out of the books. It ain't new — the twofold rising to glory or shame is Daniel's own vision, sealed in the prophets and the apostles.

threads.title: He shall convict Israel through the chosen ones of the Gentiles
threads.summary_md: Then He shall judge the Gentiles, and convict Israel through the chosen ones of the Gentiles — those who believed entering into the portion of them that fear the Lord. Paul writes the same mystery: through Israel's fall salvation came to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy, that Israel might be saved. It ain't new — that the believing nations would stir Israel to her own salvation is the apostle's mystery, foreseen here on Benjamin's deathbed.

threads.title: All Israel gathered to the Lord, the ravening wolf no more
threads.summary_md: If they walk in holiness, Benjamin says, all Israel shall be gathered unto the Lord, and he shall no longer be called a ravening wolf but a worker distributing food. Jacob's blessing had named Benjamin a wolf that ravins; Moses promised the scattered would be gathered when they returned, and Ezekiel saw the tribes made one. It ain't new — the gathering of all Israel and the turning of the wolf to a feeder is the prophets' restoration applied to Benjamin's own line.

threads.title: One beloved of the Lord shall arise, enlightening the Gentiles
threads.summary_md: Benjamin foresees one beloved of the Lord arising in the latter days, a doer of His good pleasure, enlightening the Gentiles, going to and fro among the synagogues of the nations, inscribed in the holy books, a chosen one of God for ever. Moses had called Benjamin the beloved of the Lord; and from Benjamin's seed came the apostle Paul, of that very tribe, whose work and word stand written in the scriptures and carried the light to the Gentiles. It ain't new — the beloved of Benjamin dwelling in safety is Moses' blessing, ripening into the apostle of the nations.

threads.title: Carry up my bones out of Egypt and bury me with my fathers
threads.summary_md: Benjamin's last command is the patriarchs' command: carry up my bones out of Egypt and bury me at Hebron, near my fathers — and the sons brought up the bones of all their fathers during the Canaanitish war. Joseph had bound Israel by oath to carry up his bones, Moses kept it, and they were buried in the land at the last. It ain't new — the carrying-up of the fathers' bones to the land of promise is the oath that runs from Joseph to the conquest.

threads.title: Partakers of the divine nature — the image of Elohim restored (Genesis 1, Leviticus 11, Ezekiel 36)
threads.summary_md: Peter writes that *by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust* (2 Peter 1:4). Read soberly through the covenant story, this is no promise that men become gods — it is the restoration of the image in which man was first made and the holiness to which Yahuah (LORD) calls His people. Man was formed *in our image, after our likeness* (Genesis 1:26), and again, *in the image of Elohim (God) created he him* (Genesis 1:27); the image marred by the fall is the image the precious promises renew. The *divine nature* shared is Yahuah's (the LORD's) own holiness: *ye shall be holy; for I am holy* (Leviticus 11:44) — the very command of the Torah, fulfilled in the renewed man who has *escaped the corruption that is in the world.* And the means is the new covenant promise: *A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh* (Ezekiel 36:26), with His own Spirit put within to *cause you to walk in my statutes* (Ezekiel 36:27). To partake of the divine nature is to receive that Spirit, to be made holy as He is holy, to be restored to the image of the Maker and so to keep His judgments from a heart of flesh. The share is in His holy character, not in His being; the creature is brought back to the likeness in which it was made, never lifted across the line into deity. This is sanctification, the corruption escaped and the image restored — not apotheosis.

threads.title: The ladder of virtues added to faith — the path of wisdom (Proverbs 2, Wisdom of Solomon 8)
threads.summary_md: Peter charges the elect to a chain of graces: *add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity* (2 Peter 1:5-7). This ladder is no new ethic but the path of wisdom the Hebrew books had long laid down. Proverbs sets out the same climb: seek wisdom as silver and *then shalt thou understand the fear of Yahuah (LORD), and find the knowledge of Elohim (God)* (Proverbs 2:5), *for Yahuah (LORD) giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding* (Proverbs 2:6) — the knowledge Peter bids be added to faith. And the wisdom-library names the very rungs: wisdom *teaches temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude: which are such things, as men can have nothing more profitable in their life* (Wisdom of Solomon 8:7) — Peter's temperance, patience, and godliness, the labour of wisdom herself. The diligence Peter calls for is the seeking of Proverbs 2; the virtues climbed are the virtues wisdom teaches. It ain't new: the apostle exhorts to the ancient path the restored books already walked.

threads.title: The holy mount and the Father's voice — This is my beloved Son (Psalm 2, Deuteronomy 18, Matthew 17)
threads.summary_md: Peter was an eyewitness of the majesty: *we have not followed cunningly devised fables... but were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received from Elohim (God) the Father honour and glory, when there came such a voice to him from the excellent glory, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. And this voice which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount* (2 Peter 1:16-18). The voice on the mount speaks the decree of the Psalm: *Yahuah (LORD) hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee* (Psalm 2:7) — it is the Father who declares the Son, the One enthroned upon the holy hill of Zion. And the charge that voice gave, *hear ye him,* is the charge Moses laid on Yashar'el (Israel) concerning the Prophet to come: *Yahuah Elohayka (The LORD thy God) will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken* (Deuteronomy 18:15). The gospel records the moment Peter remembers: *a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him* (Matthew 17:5). The Transfiguration is the eyewitness ground of the apostle's sure testimony. Mark the Christology: it is *Elohim (God) the Father* who gives the Son *honour and glory* and declares Him — the Father the source who declares and sends, the Son the beloved declared. No co-equal-persons grammar, no collapse of the two; the Prophet whom Moses bade Yashar'el (Israel) hearken to is the beloved Son the Father bids the world hear.

threads.title: The more sure word of prophecy — holy men moved by the Ruach HaKodesh (Psalm 119, Proverbs 30, 2 Timothy 3)
threads.summary_md: After the witness of the holy mount, Peter points the elect to a yet surer ground: *We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of Elohim (God) spake as they were moved by the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit)* (2 Peter 1:19-21). The *more sure word of prophecy* is the Tanakh — the Law and the Prophets, the Scripture *holy men of Elohim (God) spake* as the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) moved them. It is the lamp the faithful have always walked by: *Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path* (Psalm 119:105), the *light that shineth in a dark place* until the day dawns. It is no word of man but Yahuah's (the LORD's) own, fixed and enduring: *For ever, O Yahuah (LORD), thy word is settled in heaven* (Psalm 119:89). It is pure, unmixed with human will: *Every word of Elohim (God) is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him* (Proverbs 30:5). And it is the very affirmation Paul makes — the twin of this passage: *All scripture is given by inspiration of Elohim (God), and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness* (2 Timothy 3:16). What Paul calls inspired by Elohim (God), Peter calls spoken by holy men as the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) moved them: both name the Tanakh as the inspired and sure prophetic word. Peter does not set a new word over the old; he establishes the old as the more sure word — the Scripture settled in heaven, the lamp shining in the dark place, the prophecy that came not by the will of man. The Tanakh is not superseded; it is the sure word to which the elect do well to take heed until the day star arises.

threads.title: False teachers who privily deny the Master — the false prophet (Deuteronomy 13, Jude 4)
threads.summary_md: Kepha (Peter) turns to the false teachers and roots the warning in Torah: *there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying Yahuah (Lord) that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction* (2 Peter 2:1). It ain't new. Moses had already named the danger: *If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder* (Deuteronomy 13:1) — and even if the wonder comes to pass, *that prophet... shall be put to death; because he hath spoken to turn you away from Yahuah Elohaychem (the LORD your God)... to thrust thee out of the way which Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) commanded thee to walk in* (Deuteronomy 13:5). The test was never the sign but the doctrine — whether he leads you to keep the way Yahuah (LORD) commanded or turns you from it. Jude describes the very same men: *certain men crept in unawares... ungodly men, turning the grace of our Elohim (God) into lasciviousness, and denying the only Yahuah Elohim (Lord God), and our Lord Yahusha HaMashiach (Lord Jesus Christ)* (Jude 4). The false teacher who denies the Master is the false prophet of Deuteronomy 13, and his end is swift destruction.

threads.title: The angels that sinned in chains of darkness, Noah, and Sodom — the Watchers (Genesis 6, 1 Enoch, Jubilees, Jude)
threads.summary_md: To prove the certain judgment of the false teachers, Kepha (Peter) lays down three judgments the library records — and the first of them is the one the whole library keeps coming back to: *For if Elohim (God) spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment; And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly; And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample... And delivered just Lot* (2 Peter 2:4-7). The *angels that sinned* are the Watchers — the *sons of Elohim (God)* who *came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them... men of renown* (Genesis 6:4). Kepha is not coining a myth; he is reading Torah's own account of the fall that brought the Flood, and the library tells exactly how those angels were bound. Yahuah (God) commanded, *Bind Azâzêl hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness* (1 Enoch 10:4), and of Semjâzâ, *bind them fast for seventy generations in the valleys of the earth, till the day of their judgement* (1 Enoch 10:12) — the very *chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment.* Enoch was shown the place itself: *And he said unto me: ‘This place is the prison of the angels, and here they will be imprisoned for ever.’* (1 Enoch 21:10). Jubilees agrees to the word: Elohim (God) *bade us to bind them in the depths of the earth, and behold they are bound* (Jubilees 5:6), *bound in the depths of the earth for ever, until the day of the great condemnation* (Jubilees 5:10). This is the same Watchers record Kepha (Peter) leaned on in his first letter (1 Peter 3:19-20) and Jude leans on in his: *the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day* (Jude 6). Then the Flood: *Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark* (Genesis 7:23), *Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations* (Genesis 6:9) — *Noah the eighth person,* the few *saved by water* (1 Peter 3:20), the days of Noah the Master made the type of his coming (Matthew 24:37). Then Sodom: *Yahuah (LORD) rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire... and he overthrew those cities* (Genesis 19:24-25), *set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire* (Jude 7); and just Lot delivered when *they brought him forth, and set him without the city* (Genesis 19:16). The Hebrew library catalogues every one of these: *the earth being drowned with the flood, wisdom again preserved it... in a piece of wood* (Wisdom 10:4), *she delivered the righteous man, who fled from the fire which fell down upon the five cities* (Wisdom 10:6), and in the same order Kepha keeps — *the old giants, who fell away* (Sirach 16:7), the place of Lot not spared (Sirach 16:8), Noah *left as a remnant to the earth, when the flood came* (Sirach 44:17). The lesson is one: *Yahuah (Lord) knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished* (2 Peter 2:9). The angels that sinned, the old world, the cities of the plain — the judgment-history the whole library records, and the false teachers stand in its line.

threads.title: Angels greater in power bring not a railing accusation (Jude 9)
threads.summary_md: Kepha (Peter) marks the presumption of the false teachers, who *are not afraid to speak evil of dignities* (2 Peter 2:10), by contrast with the holy angels: *Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before Yahuah (Lord)* (2 Peter 2:11). Jude gives the very case in point: *Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, Yahuah (Lord) rebuke thee* (Jude 9). If the mightiest angel withholds the railing word and leaves the rebuke to Yahuah (Lord) himself, how reckless are the brute men who speak evil of the things they do not understand. The twin letters teach the same restraint — judgment belongs to Yahuah (Lord), not to the railing tongue.

threads.title: The way of Balaam the son of Bosor and the dumb ass (Numbers 22, 31, Deuteronomy 23, Jude 11)
threads.summary_md: Kepha (Peter) names the false teachers by an old example: they *have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness; But was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet* (2 Peter 2:15-16). The scene is Numbers 22: when the seer could not see the angel his beast had seen, *Yahuah (LORD) opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?* (Numbers 22:28); and only then *Yahuah (LORD) opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of Yahuah (LORD) standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand* (Numbers 22:31). The dumb beast saw clearer than the prophet greedy for reward — *the madness of the prophet* forbidden by an ass. And the way of Balaam is not merely the curse-for-hire but the counsel that followed: *these caused the children of Yashar'el (Israel), through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against Yahuah (LORD) in the matter of Peor* (Numbers 31:16) — the hireling who, unable to curse, taught Moab to seduce the people into sin. Torah remembers him as the prophet *hired... to curse* (Deuteronomy 23:4), yet *Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) would not hearken unto Balaam; but... turned the curse into a blessing* (Deuteronomy 23:5). Jude marks the same way: they *ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward* (Jude 11). The way of Balaam is the way of the prophet for hire — and it ends, as Balaam ended, under the drawn sword.

threads.title: The dog is turned to his own vomit again (Proverbs 26)
threads.summary_md: Kepha (Peter) closes the chapter with a proverb named outright. The false teachers who *escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of Yahuah (Lord) and Saviour Yahusha HaMashiach (Jesus Christ)* and are *again entangled therein, and overcome* (2 Peter 2:20) have proved the wisdom of the fathers: *it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire* (2 Peter 2:22). The proverb is Solomon's: *As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly* (Proverbs 26:11). The one who turns *from the holy commandment delivered unto them* (2 Peter 2:21) — the Torah-rooted way of righteousness — returns to the very corruption he had left, the washed sow to her mire, the dog to his vomit. Better never to have known the way than, knowing it, to turn back.

threads.title: Scoffers in the last days: Where is the promise of his coming? (Isaiah 5, Malachi 2, Ezekiel 12)
threads.summary_md: Peter warns *that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation* (2 Peter 3:3-4). The taunt is ancient, not new. Isaiah's mockers dared the judgment to come if it were real: *Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Yashar'el (Israel) draw nigh and come, that we may know it!* (Isaiah 5:19). Malachi named the same doubt: *Ye have wearied Yahuah (LORD) with your words... When ye say... Where is the Elohim (God) of judgment?* (Malachi 2:17). And Ezekiel records the very proverb of the scoffers: *what is that proverb that ye have in the land of Yashar'el (Israel), saying, The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth?* (Ezekiel 12:22) — the same *all things continue* that Peter's scoffers speak. But Yahuah (LORD) answered Ezekiel: *The days are at hand, and the effect of every vision* (Ezekiel 12:23). The prolonging is not the failing of the word but the longsuffering of the One who keeps it; the mockery against the sure prophetic word is old, and it has always been answered by the day that comes.

threads.title: By the word of Elohim (God) the heavens were of old (Genesis 1, Psalm 33)
threads.summary_md: Against the scoffers' *all things continue as they were,* Peter sets creation by the spoken word: *For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of Elohim (God) the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water* (2 Peter 3:5). At the beginning Elohim (God) ordered the waters by his word — *Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters* (Genesis 1:6) — and brought the dry land out: *Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so* (Genesis 1:9). The Psalm states the principle outright: *By the word of Yahuah (LORD) were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth* (Psalm 33:6). The heavens are not self-existing nor everlasting in themselves; they were framed by the word and *standing out of the water,* and *the same word* now keeps them *in store, reserved unto fire* (2 Peter 3:7). What the word made, the word governs — and the word can dissolve and remake. The scoffer who says nothing changes has forgotten the word that spoke the world into being.

threads.title: The world that then was, overflowed with water, perished (Genesis 7, Jubilees 5, Wisdom 14)
threads.summary_md: The word that framed the world also unmade it once. Peter answers the scoffers with the Flood: *Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished* (2 Peter 3:6). Genesis tells how the waters that creation had divided returned: *the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened* (Genesis 7:11), until *every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground... and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark* (Genesis 7:23). The restored library records the same judgment in the same imagery: *Yahuah (God) opened seven flood-gates of heaven, And the mouths of the fountains of the great deep... until the whole world was full of water* (Jubilees 5:23). And the wisdom of the library remembers it as the perishing of the proud while the remnant was carried through: *when the proud giants perished, the hope of the world governed by your hand escaped in a weak vessel, and left to all ages a seed of generation* (Wisdom of Solomon 14:6). One world framed out of the water was unmade by water at the word of Elohim (God) — the down-payment of the day of judgment to come, *reserved unto fire* (2 Peter 3:7). The judgment the scoffers deny is written across the whole library; it ain't new.

threads.title: One day is with Yahuah (Lord) as a thousand years (Psalm 90)
threads.summary_md: To the charge that the promise has failed because it tarries, Peter answers with Moses' reckoning of time: *be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with Yahuah (Lord) as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day* (2 Peter 3:8). The psalm of Moses said it first: *For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night* (Psalm 90:4). What the scoffer counts as long delay is no delay to the Everlasting, in whose sight a thousand years pass as a single day. And the seeming slowness is mercy, not slackness: *Yahuah (Lord) is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance* (2 Peter 3:9). The prolonging of the days is the patience of the One who keeps the sure word — the very longsuffering Peter goes on to call *salvation* (2 Peter 3:15).

threads.title: The day of Yahuah (Lord) as a thief; the elements melt with fervent heat (Isaiah 13, Joel 2, Malachi 4)
threads.summary_md: *But the day of Yahuah (Lord) will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up* (2 Peter 3:10). This is no new doctrine but the prophets' own day of Yahuah, handed on. Isaiah cried *Howl ye; for the day of Yahuah (LORD) is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty* (Isaiah 13:6), the day that *cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate* (Isaiah 13:9), wherein *I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place* (Isaiah 13:13). Joel sounded the alarm: *Blow ye the trumpet in Zion... for the day of Yahuah (LORD) cometh, for it is nigh at hand* (Joel 2:1). Malachi named its fire: *the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud... shall be stubble... shall burn them up* (Malachi 4:1) — the very *day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men* (2 Peter 3:7) in which *the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved* (2 Peter 3:12). And Paul taught the same to the Thessalonians in Peter's exact words: *the day of Yahuah (Lord) so cometh as a thief in the night* (1 Thessalonians 5:2), for which cause Peter calls him *our beloved brother* whose epistles speak *of these things* (2 Peter 3:15-16). The shaking of the heavens, the burning oven, the thief in the night — one day, one Judge, one sure prophetic word against the scoffers' false peace.

threads.title: New heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness (Isaiah 65, Isaiah 66, Revelation 21)
threads.summary_md: The day of fire is not the end of the story. *Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness* (2 Peter 3:13). The promise is Yahuah's (LORD) own, spoken through Isaiah: *For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind* (Isaiah 65:17). And Isaiah binds the new creation to the enduring of the covenant seed: *For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith Yahuah (LORD), so shall your seed and your name remain* (Isaiah 66:22). This is no new people in a severed story but the seed and name of the covenant abiding forever in the world made new. John beheld the promise fulfilled: *And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea* (Revelation 21:1). The same word that framed the heavens of old, that drowned the world that then was, and that reserves the present heavens unto fire, remakes them new — and *righteousness dwelleth* there. The prophets promised it, Peter waits for it, John beholds it: one consummation of the one covenant story.

threads.title: Thou art a shield for me — my glory, and the lifter up of mine head
threads.summary_md: The superscription names the scene: *A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son*. The king is driven from his own city by his own son — *the conspiracy was strong; for the people increased continually with Absalom* (2 Samuel 15:12) — and David's word is *Arise, and let us flee; for we shall not else escape from Absalom* (2 Samuel 15:14). So the psalm opens, *Yahuah (LORD), how are they increased that trouble me! many are they that rise up against me* (Psalm 3:1). On the road the taunt *Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in Elohim (God)* (3:2) is spoken in the flesh: Shimei comes out cursing, *thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial* (2 Samuel 16:7), declaring *Yahuah (LORD) hath delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom thy son* (2 Samuel 16:8) — the living voice of the mockers who say Yahuah has cast the king off. But the king answers them not with the sword but with Yahuah: *But thou, O Yahuah (LORD), art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head* (3:3); *I cried unto Yahuah (LORD) with my voice, and he heard me out of his holy hill* (3:4). The shield about him is the shield first named to Abram — *Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward* (Genesis 15:1) — and the shield Moses blessed the whole people by: *Happy art thou, O Yashar'el (Israel)... O people saved by Yahuah (LORD), the shield of thy help... and thine enemies shall be found liars unto thee* (Deuteronomy 33:29). The covenant shield of Abraham and of all Yashar'el (Israel) is the one shield about the hunted king, and the enemies who said there was no help for him are found liars.

threads.title: I laid me down and slept; I awaked — for Yahuah sustained me
threads.summary_md: In the night of the flight, hunted and surrounded, David says *I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for Yahuah (LORD) sustained me* (Psalm 3:5). The lying-down-and-rising is read by the fathers as a resurrection figure — the One who lays down and rises because Yahuah does not abandon him. The same David sings the figure plainly: *my flesh also shall rest in hope. For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption* (Psalm 16:9-10) — the rest that is no defeat, the soul not left in the grave, the Holy One who does not see corruption. Forward, the Formed Son speaks the very figure in his own mouth: *Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again* (John 10:17); *No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father* (John 10:18). And the Father raises him: *Whom Elohim (God) hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it* (Acts 2:24). The sleeper sustained through the night, the flesh that rests in hope, the Son who lays down his life and takes it again — one figure: he lies down and rises by the Father's sustaining; he is Yahuah's own, and he has a Father.

threads.title: Salvation belongeth unto Yahuah — thy blessing is upon thy people
threads.summary_md: The psalm closes giving all the deliverance to Yahuah alone: *Salvation belongeth unto Yahuah (LORD): thy blessing is upon thy people* (Psalm 3:8). The king who *will not be afraid of ten thousands of people* (3:6) and cries *Arise, O Yahuah (LORD); save me, O my Elohim (God)* (3:7) ascribes the whole victory to Yahuah, not to his own arm. Jonah, swallowed in the deep, confesses the same out of the fish's belly: *I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay that that I have vowed. Salvation is of Yahuah (LORD)* (Jonah 2:9). And it is the very song the redeemed cry before the throne: *Salvation to our Elohim (God) which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb* (Revelation 7:10); *Alleluia; Salvation, and glory, and honour, and power, unto Yahuah Eloheinu (the Lord our God)* (Revelation 19:1). The hunted king, the prophet in the deep, and the great multitude in heaven all confess one thing: salvation is Yahuah's gift, never won by the strength of man — and *thy blessing is upon thy people*.

threads.title: Stand in awe, and sin not — Paul takes up the psalm word for word
threads.summary_md: The heart of the evening psalm is a night-discipline of the heart: *Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah* (Psalm 4:4). Paul takes it up word for word: *Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath* (Ephesians 4:26) — the same awe-or-anger held under the same restraint (*sin not*), at the same evening hour (*upon your bed* answered by *let not the sun go down*). This is not a new commandment replacing an old one; it is the apostle quoting the psalter's own instruction, the Torah-rooted discipline of the still and examined heart carried forward unbroken. The restored witness sings the same posture: *They that fear Yahuah (God) will prepare their hearts, and humble their souls in his sight* (Sirach 2:17) — the heart communed-with upon the bed, prepared and humbled, stilled in awe before Yahuah. Stand in awe; commune with your own heart; be still; and sin not.

threads.title: Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in Yahuah
threads.summary_md: *Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in Yahuah (LORD)* (Psalm 4:5). The phrase is Torah's own — the blessing of Zebulun and Issachar at the mountain: *They shall call the people unto the mountain; there they shall offer sacrifices of righteousness* (Deuteronomy 33:19). And the psalter defines what that sacrifice IS at heart, lest any reduce it to ritual: *The sacrifices of Elohim (God) are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O Elohim (God), thou wilt not despise* (Psalm 51:17). The sacrifice of righteousness is the worship of the trusting, contrite heart — offering AND trust together, never offering without trust nor trust without offering. The NT keeps the very category, never abolishing the altar but naming its abiding fruit: *By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to Elohim (God) continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name* (Hebrews 13:15). The sacrifices of righteousness are the continual praise of the heart that puts its trust in Yahuah.

threads.title: Yahuah hath set apart him that is godly for himself
threads.summary_md: *But know that Yahuah (LORD) hath set apart him that is godly for himself: Yahuah (LORD) will hear when I call unto him* (Psalm 4:3). Over against the *sons of men* who *love vanity, and seek after leasing* (4:2), the godly one is set apart — claimed by Yahuah for Himself, and heard when he calls. The NT seals this same set-apart godliness with a double mark: *Nevertheless the foundation of Elohim (God) standeth sure, having this seal, Yahuah (Lord) knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Messiah (Christ) depart from iniquity* (2 Timothy 2:19). The two clauses are the two halves of Psalm 4:3 — Yahuah KNOWS them that are His (He *hath set apart him that is godly for himself*), and His own DEPART from iniquity (the godly, not the lovers of vanity). He who is set apart for Yahuah is heard when he calls, and walks apart from sin.

threads.title: Lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us — the Aaronic blessing prayed back
threads.summary_md: When the many ask *Who will shew us any good?*, the psalmist answers by praying the priestly benediction back to Yahuah: *Yahuah (LORD), lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us* (Psalm 4:6). This is the Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6 turned into petition: *Yahuah (LORD) make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee* (Numbers 6:25); *Yahuah (LORD) lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace* (Numbers 6:26). The shining, lifted face is the good the trusting heart seeks — greater than any harvest, for the gladness follows: *Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased* (4:7). And the lifted countenance gives PEACE — the very peace in which the psalm closes: *I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep* (4:8). The light of the face is the answer to *who will shew us any good?*

threads.title: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep — Yahuah only makest me dwell in safety
threads.summary_md: The evening psalm closes in the peace of trust: *I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Yahuah (LORD), only makest me dwell in safety* (Psalm 4:8). It is the twin of the morning psalm's waking — *I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for Yahuah (LORD) sustained me* (Psalm 3:5) — the same sustaining hand keeping the godly asleep and awake. The fearless sleep is the covenant peace Torah promises the obedient: *And I will give peace in the land, and ye shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid* (Leviticus 26:6); and the proverb seals it for the one who walks in trust: *When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet* (Proverbs 3:24). The one set apart for Yahuah (4:3), who offers the sacrifices of righteousness and trusts (4:5), and prays the light of the countenance (4:6), lies down without fear — for Yahuah ALONE makes him dwell in safety.

threads.title: Their throat is an open sepulchre — the none-righteous catena that establishes the law
threads.summary_md: In the morning prayer David lays bare the workers of iniquity: *For there is no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part is very wickedness; their throat is an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue* (Psalm 5:9). Paul lifts this very phrase into the catena by which he proves all under sin: *Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips* (Romans 3:13). The *there is none righteous, no, not one* (Romans 3:10) twin of this catena — Psalm 14:1-3 / Psalm 53:1-3 — is already woven live; Psalm 5:9 is the open-sepulchre line of the same indictment. The point of the lens is how Paul ENDS the argument. He exposes the deceitful mouth *that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before Elohim (God)* (Romans 3:19) — and then, far from voiding the Torah, he upholds it: *Do we then make void the law through faith? Elohim (God) forbid: yea, we establish the law* (Romans 3:31). The diagnosis of sin that quotes David's psalm is the diagnosis that ESTABLISHES the covenant instruction; the open-sepulchre tongue is condemned by the very law the catena confirms standing.

threads.title: Thou art not a Elohim that hath pleasure in wickedness — neither shall evil dwell with thee
threads.summary_md: The morning prayer rests on Yahuah's holiness: *For thou art not a Elohim (God) that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee. The foolish shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity* (Psalm 5:4-5). This is Habakkuk's own ground of appeal against the violence of his day: *Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity* (Habakkuk 1:13) — Yahuah cannot look on iniquity, and evil cannot dwell with Him. And the holiness that excludes evil from His presence is consummated FORWARD in the holy city: *And there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth, neither whatsoever worketh abomination, or maketh a lie: but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life* (Revelation 21:27). The *bloody and deceitful man* (Psalm 5:6) and the open-sepulchre tongue (5:9) are exactly what is shut out — from the morning prayer to the New Jerusalem, no evil dwells where Yahuah dwells, for He is *of purer eyes than to behold evil*.

threads.title: The foolish shall not stand in thy sight — the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment
threads.summary_md: *The foolish shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity* (Psalm 5:5). This is Psalm 1's closing verdict in another key: *Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous* (Psalm 1:5). The workers of iniquity — the foolish, the ungodly, the sinners — cannot stand where Yahuah is, neither in His sight in the morning prayer nor in the judgment and the congregation of the righteous. The whole psalter opens (Psalm 1) and prays (Psalm 5) on the same divide between the righteous who stand and the wicked who cannot.

threads.title: Thou wilt bless the righteous — with favour compass him as with a shield
threads.summary_md: The prayer ends in benediction on those who trust: *But let all those that put their trust in thee rejoice: let them ever shout for joy, because thou defendest them: let them also that love thy name be joyful in thee. For thou, Yahuah (LORD), wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield* (Psalm 5:11-12). The favour that compasses the righteous like a shield is the psalter's steady confession: *For Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) is a sun and shield: Yahuah (LORD) will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly. O Yahuah Tseva'ot (LORD of hosts), blessed is the man that trusteth in thee* (Psalm 84:11-12). And David has already named it in the morning psalm before: *But thou, O Yahuah (LORD), art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head* (Psalm 3:3). The blessing on the righteous is not a thing Yahuah gives apart from Himself — He IS the shield; the one who trusts is the one He compasses about with favour.

threads.title: They flatter with their tongue — the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul
threads.summary_md: David prays against the deceitful tongue: *Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: Yahuah (LORD) will abhor the bloody and deceitful man* (Psalm 5:6); *there is no faithfulness in their mouth... their throat is an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue* (Psalm 5:9). The wisdom of the restored library warns of this very mouth: *Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:11). The flattering, lying tongue is not merely a thing Yahuah abhors — it slays the very soul that wields it. The deceitful man Yahuah destroys is the man whose lying mouth has already destroyed himself.

threads.title: Rebuke me not in thine anger — the chastening that heals, never the curse
threads.summary_md: The first of the seven Penitential Psalms opens with a plea that is the verbatim twin of the next penitential psalm: *O Yahuah (LORD), rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure* (Psalm 6:1) — *O Yahuah (LORD), rebuke me not in thy wrath: neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure* (Psalm 38:1). Read through the framework, this is not a request to escape correction but to receive it as a Father's rod and not as the consuming covenant-wrath. The curse is the Deuteronomy-28 wrath upon covenant-breaking; the chastening is the love that heals rather than crushes: *Have mercy upon me, O Yahuah (LORD); for I am weak: O Yahuah (LORD), heal me; for my bones are vexed* (6:2). The ground of the appeal is mercy, never merit: *Return, O Yahuah (LORD), deliver my soul: oh save me for thy mercies' sake* (6:4). The same hand that wounds in correction binds up — the psalmist asks the Father to temper the rod, not to lay it down.

threads.title: In death there is no remembrance of thee — the living praise, the dead are silent
threads.summary_md: At the floor of the penitent's prayer is the Sheol-silence motif: *For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?* (Psalm 6:5). It is the psalter's recurring argument from the edge of the pit — praise belongs to the living, so spare me to praise thee. *What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit? Shall the dust praise thee? shall it declare thy truth?* (Psalm 30:9); *Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee?... Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction?... in the land of forgetfulness?* (Psalm 88:10-12); *The dead praise not Yahuah (LORD), neither any that go down into silence* (Psalm 115:17). Hezekiah prays it at the gates of the grave and is granted fifteen years: *the grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee... The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day* (Isaiah 38:18-19). The restored wisdom-witnesses sing the same: *Who shall praise the Most High in the grave, instead of them which live and give thanks? Thanksgiving perishes from the dead... the living and sound in heart shall praise Yahuah (God)* (Sirach 17:27-28); *the dead that are in the graves... will give to Yahuah (God) neither praise nor righteousness: But the soul that is greatly vexed... will give you praise* (Baruch 2:17-18) — and Baruch's *soul that is greatly vexed* is the psalmist's own *soul... sore vexed* (6:3). The whole canon holds one motif: praise is the breath of the living; the resurrection of the body is what finally fills the silence — the answer Psalm 6 reaches toward but does not yet see.

threads.title: Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity — the psalmist's word on the Formed Son's lips
threads.summary_md: The penitent's prayer turns the moment it is heard: *Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for Yahuah (LORD) hath heard the voice of my weeping* (Psalm 6:8); *Yahuah (LORD) hath heard my supplication; Yahuah (LORD) will receive my prayer* (6:9). And Yahusha (Jesus) takes the psalmist's very word onto his own lips in the judgment: *And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity* (Matthew 7:23); *But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity* (Luke 13:27). Read through the Formed and the Formless: the One who speaks the dismissal at the shut door speaks Psalm 6's own line — the Formed Son who *hath heard the voice of my weeping* is the same Yahuah to whom this psalm cried, and he has a Father. And the Torah-filter (1 John 2:3-4) names who is sent away: in Matthew 7 the dismissed are those who prophesied and cast out devils in the Name yet *work iniquity* — anomia, lawlessness — not the law-keepers. The psalm's *workers of iniquity* and the judgment's *workers of iniquity* are measured by the same standard, and the weeping that is heard is the cry that is received.

threads.title: Yahuah shall judge the people — the righteous Judge angry with the wicked every day
threads.summary_md: David, hunted, will not raise his own hand against the persecutor; he hales the whole matter before the bench of heaven: *Yahuah (LORD) shall judge the people: judge me, O Yahuah (LORD), according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me* (Psalm 7:8). The Judge he appeals to is no idle one — *Elohim (God) judgeth the righteous, and Elohim (God) is angry with the wicked every day* (7:11). Read FORWARD through the Formed and the Formless: the formless Father has set His judgment into the hand of the Formed Son — *the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son* (John 5:22), *and hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of Adam* (John 5:27). The seed-of-Adam weight is the warrant: the One who took flesh from Adam's own line is the One ordained to judge Adam's race — *he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead* (Acts 17:31). And the daily anger of 7:11 is the wrath the impenitent store against themselves — *thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of Elohim (God); Who will render to every man according to his deeds* (Romans 2:5-6). The just man's plea — *judge me... according to my righteousness* — is answered at that seat: the righteous Judge establishes the just and renders to the wicked his own.

threads.title: The righteous Elohim trieth the hearts and reins
threads.summary_md: The Judge of Psalm 7 is no respecter of the surface the wicked trusts in. David's plea rests on a Judge who reads the inward man: *Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end; but establish the just: for the righteous Elohim (God) trieth the hearts and reins* (Psalm 7:9). This is the very ground Jeremiah stands on against his own persecutors — *O Yahuah Tseva'ot (LORD of hosts), that judgest righteously, that triest the reins and the heart, let me see thy vengeance on them: for unto thee have I revealed my cause* (Jeremiah 11:20) — and which Yahuah declares to be His own steady office — *I Yahuah (LORD) search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings* (Jeremiah 17:10). At David's own anointing Yahuah taught it: *man looketh on the outward appearance, but Yahuah (LORD) looketh on the heart* (1 Samuel 16:7). And the Formed Son claims the office FORWARD in His own voice — *all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works* (Revelation 2:23). The heart-trier of the psalm is the heart-searcher on the throne; He renders to every man not by the show but by what the reins conceal. He is Yahuah, and He has a Father.

threads.title: He made a pit, and is fallen into the ditch which he made — the mischief returns on his own head
threads.summary_md: The wicked man of Psalm 7 arms himself and conceives violence — *he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood* (7:14) — and then his own engine turns on him: *He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate* (7:15-16).
