threads.summary_md: The chapter turns from judgment to mercy, and names the Redeemer who walked with his people: *In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them: in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; and he bare them, and carried them all the days of old* (Isaiah 63:9). Who is this Angel of his Presence who SAVED, BORE, and CARRIED Yashar'el (Israel)? The Torah names him. *Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared* (Exodus 23:20) — and the next word is the load-bearing one: *Beware of him, and obey his voice, provoke him not; for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him* (23:21). An Angel who carries the Name itself, who can pardon or refuse to pardon transgression, is no created messenger. He is the visible Yahuah, the Formed Son. He is the same Presence who delivered at the sea: *the angel of Elohim (God), which went before the camp of Yashar'el (Israel), removed and went behind them; and the pillar of the cloud... stood behind them* (Exodus 14:19). And he first appeared from the bush: *the angel of Yahuah (LORD) appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush* (Exodus 3:2) — and is then called Yahuah and Elohim outright, the One who *surely seen the affliction of my people* and *come down to deliver them* (Exodus 3:7-8). The Angel of his Presence who bears the Name, who appeared and spoke and led and bore Yashar'el all the days of old, is the Formed Son — the expressed Word drawn from the Formless Father, the pre-incarnate Redeemer present with his people, who later took on flesh.

threads.title: They vexed his holy Spirit — grieving Yahuah's own presence
threads.summary_md: The mercy turns to grief: *But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them* (Isaiah 63:10). The plea then remembers the days when the Spirit was among them: *Where is he that brought them up out of the sea with the shepherd of his flock? where is he that put his holy Spirit within him?* (63:11), *the Spirit of Yahuah (LORD) caused him to rest* (63:14). This holy Spirit is Yahuah's own presence and power among his people — not a third co-equal person. To vex the Spirit is to grieve Yahuah himself. Paul warns against the very thing Yashar'el did: *And grieve not the holy Spirit of Elohim (God), whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption* (Ephesians 4:30). And Stephen names the identical rebellion across the generations: *Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit): as your fathers did, so do ye* (Acts 7:51). The fathers who vexed the Spirit in the wilderness and the generation that resists him still are grieving one Spirit — the abiding presence of Yahuah, the same Spirit who led them through the deep and gave them rest.

threads.title: Thou, O Yahuah, art our father, our redeemer — the one Yahuah
threads.summary_md: The penitent plea rises to the Father: *Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Yashar'el (Israel) acknowledge us not: thou, O Yahuah (LORD), art our father, our redeemer; thy name is from everlasting* (Isaiah 63:16). The Redeemer who trod the winepress and the Angel who bore them all the days of old is also the Father — the one Yahuah, whose Name is from everlasting. The Messiah teaches his people that same address: *After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name* (Matthew 6:9). The everlasting Name of the Father-Redeemer is the Name hallowed in the prayer. And the plea is the cry of the gathered tribes: *Return for thy servants' sake, the tribes of thine inheritance* (63:17) — the two houses, the whole inheritance, crying to the Father-Redeemer who saved them, bore them, and carried them, whose Name is from everlasting and whose mercies do not fail.

threads.title: Whoso despiseth the word shall be destroyed — but he that feareth the commandment shall be rewarded
threads.summary_md: The framework weight of the chapter sits on the word: *Whoso despiseth the word shall be destroyed: but he that feareth the commandment shall be rewarded* (Proverbs 13:13), sealed by *The law of the wise is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death* (13:14). To despise the word is no small matter — the Torah itself pronounces the verdict word for word: *Because he hath despised the word of Yahuah (LORD), and hath broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off; his iniquity shall be upon him* (Numbers 15:31). The proverb is not a new sentence but the law of Moses set as a couplet. The Chronicler shows the verdict carried out on a whole nation: *they mocked the messengers of Elohim (God), and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of Yahuah (LORD) arose against his people, till there was no remedy* (2 Chronicles 36:16) — the despised word brought the exile, the very *destroyed* the proverb names. And the reward half is stated plain by the same book: *He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul* (19:16). The law is never the curse; it is a fountain of life, the guard of the soul. To despise the word is destruction; to fear the commandment is reward.

threads.title: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick — but the desire come is a tree of life
threads.summary_md: The chapter turns fulfilled longing into a figure that runs the whole canon: *Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life* (Proverbs 13:12), echoed by *The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul* (13:19). The tree of life was planted in the garden — *the tree of life also in the midst of the garden* (Genesis 2:9) — and Adam was barred from it; the heart sick with deferred hope is the heart east of Eden, longing for the life it lost. Proverbs makes wisdom herself that tree: *She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her* (3:18); *The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life* (11:30); *A wholesome tongue is a tree of life* (15:4). To grasp wisdom is to grasp the tree, and the desire that at last comes is a foretaste of its fruit. And the book closes on the tree restored: *In the midst of the street of it... was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits... and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations* (Revelation 22:2) — barred at Eden, opened again in the City, where *they that do his commandments... may have right to the tree of life* (22:14). The deferred hope of the whole creation comes at last, and it is the tree of life.

threads.title: He that spareth his rod hateth his son — the Father's loving chastening
threads.summary_md: The chapter binds discipline to love: *He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes* (Proverbs 13:24). The rod is not cruelty but care — and the pattern is the Father's own with His sons. Proverbs says it again and again: *despise not the chastening of Yahuah (LORD)... for whom Yahuah (LORD) loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth* (3:11-12); *the rod of correction shall drive it far from him* (22:15); *Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell* (23:14); *The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame* (29:15). The seeming hardness is mercy at its root — the rod is wielded to deliver the soul, and the father who withholds it does not love but hates, abandoning the son to a worse end. The restored witness keeps the same word: *He that loves his son causeth him oft to feel the rod, that he may have joy of him in the end* (Sirach 30:1); *He that chastiseth his son shall have joy in him* (30:2). And the NT lifts the proverb straight up to the Father: *whom Yahuah (Lord) loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth* (Hebrews 12:6); *what son is he whom the father chasteneth not?* (12:7) — the unchastened is no true son. The counter-charge guards the measure: *ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of Yahuah (Lord)* (Ephesians 6:4) — neither sparing the rod (which is hate) nor provoking to wrath (which is cruelty), but raising the child in the Father's own admonition.

threads.title: The light of the righteous rejoiceth — but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out
threads.summary_md: The chapter sets two lights side by side: *The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out* (Proverbs 13:9). Job's friends and Job alike know the put-out lamp — Bildad: *the light of the wicked shall be put out, and the spark of his fire shall not shine* (Job 18:5); Job: *How oft is the candle of the wicked put out!* (21:17) — and Proverbs seals it: *the candle of the wicked shall be put out* (24:20). The wicked man's lamp is a borrowed flame with no oil of righteousness to feed it; it gutters and goes dark. The righteous light, by contrast, is Yahuah's own sowing: *Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart* (Psalm 97:11) — not a flame they kindle but one sown for them, springing up to gladness, a light that does not go out. And the NT sets that light on a stand: *Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid* (Matthew 5:14); *let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven* (5:16). The righteous light is meant to shine and be seen — never hid, never snuffed like the lamp of the wicked.

threads.title: Rich yet nothing, poor yet great riches — and the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just
threads.summary_md: The chapter weighs true riches against false: *There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches* (Proverbs 13:7), with *Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase* (13:11) and *A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just* (13:22). Qoheleth groaned over the heaped wealth he must surrender: *I hated all my labour... because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me* (Ecclesiastes 2:18) — and he named the very transfer the proverb foretells: *to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before Elohim (God)* (2:26). Job saw the same: *He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver* (27:17). The self-made rich man trusts what he cannot keep — *He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch* (Proverbs 11:28). The restored witness draws the hoarder's portrait: *now will eat continually of my goods; and yet he knoweth not what time shall come upon him, and that he must leave those things to others, and die* (Sirach 11:19). And Yahusha (Jesus) tells the parable plain — *So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward Elohim (God)* (Luke 12:21) — while the risen Master rebukes the church that boasts its goods: *thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor* (Revelation 3:17). Paul holds the whole paradox: *as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things* (2 Corinthians 6:10). To be rich before men and bare before Yahuah is to have nothing; to be poor before men and rich toward Elohim is to possess all.

threads.title: Evil pursueth sinners — but to the righteous good shall be repaid
threads.summary_md: The chapter states the law of recompense: *Evil pursueth sinners: but to the righteous good shall be repayed* (Proverbs 13:21). This is no random outcome but Yahuah's settled order, stated by the same book in the prior chapter: *Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner* (11:31); and the evil catches the wicked however they league together — *Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered* (11:21) — the good repaid reaching even to the line of the righteous. David sings the two ways side by side: *Many sorrows shall be to the wicked: but he that trusteth in Yahuah (LORD), mercy shall compass him about* (Psalm 32:10). The evil a man sows turns and pursues him; the good repaid the righteous is the mercy that compasses the one who trusts.

threads.title: There is a way which seemeth right — but the end thereof are the ways of death
threads.summary_md: The chapter's keystone is the two-ways verse: *There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death* (Proverbs 14:12). The deceit is the SEEMING — the way looks right to the man walking it, yet its end is death. So weighty is the warning that the book records it twice, word for word: *There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death* (16:25). The same book names the root of the error — *The way of a fool is right in his own eyes* (12:15) — and its cure — *Trust in Yahuah (LORD) with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding* (3:5), *Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear Yahuah (LORD), and depart from evil* (3:7). Judges shows a whole nation on the seems-right road: *In those days there was no king in Yashar'el (Israel): every man did that which was right in his own eyes* (21:25). Isaiah lifts the contrast to its height — *my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith Yahuah (LORD)* (55:8); *as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways* (55:9) — the way that seems right to a man is simply not Yahuah's way. The New Testament keeps the two-ways exactly, never softening it: *wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat... strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it* (Matthew 7:13-14); *the end of those things is death... the wages of sin is death; but the gift of Elohim (God) is eternal life* (Romans 6:21,23). And the one Way that does not merely seem right is named by the Formed Son: *I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me* (John 14:6). Every way that seems right to a man ends in death; the way to the Father is the one He IS. (A parallel Proverbs-12 two-ways thread gathers 14:12 and 16:25 among its members; this thread is the same one testimony anchored here in chapter 14 — reinforcing it, not copying.)

threads.title: He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker
threads.summary_md: The chapter binds the treatment of the poor straight to the honour of Yahuah: *He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor* (Proverbs 14:31). The poor man is made in the image of Yahuah, so to crush him is to reproach the One who made him, and to show him mercy is to honour that same Maker. The book says it twice — *Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker* (17:5) — and names the common Maker — *The rich and poor meet together: Yahuah (LORD) is the maker of them all* (22:2). Job lived by it — *Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?* (31:15) — for behind it all stands the image stamped at creation: *So Elohim (God) created man in his own image, in the image of Elohim (God) created he him* (Genesis 1:27). The mercy half becomes a transaction with Yahuah Himself — *He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto Yahuah (LORD); and that which he hath given will he pay him again* (19:17) — and the King consummates both halves at the judgment: *Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me* (Matthew 25:40); *Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me* (Matthew 25:45). To honour the Maker is to have mercy on the poor; to oppress the poor is to reproach Him to His face.

threads.title: Righteousness exalteth a nation — but sin is a reproach to any people
threads.summary_md: The chapter sets the destiny of a whole people on a single measure: *Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people* (Proverbs 14:34). This is the Deuteronomy 28 blessing-and-curse stated as a proverb. Obedience lifts the nation: *if thou shalt hearken diligently unto the voice of Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God), to observe and to do all his commandments... Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) will set thee on high above all nations of the earth* (Deuteronomy 28:1). Disobedience is the reproach: *if thou wilt not hearken... that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee* (28:15). The exalting rests on covenant, not on power — *Blessed is the nation whose Elohim (God) is Yahuah (LORD); and the people whom he hath chosen for his own inheritance* (Psalm 33:12). The same dynamic governs the city and the rule: *By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked* (Proverbs 11:11); *When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn* (Proverbs 29:2). The chosen nation here is Yashar'el (Israel), the covenant people — never a replacement people grafted in by confession. Righteousness, the kept Torah, exalts; sin, the forsaken covenant, is the reproach. The proverb is the covenant law written small.

threads.title: In the fear of Yahuah is strong confidence — a fountain of life
threads.summary_md: The chapter carries the book's great motto in two couplets: *In the fear of Yahuah (LORD) is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge* (Proverbs 14:26), and *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death* (14:27). The fear of Yahuah is no cringing dread but the ground of confidence and the very fountain of life. It is the book's inclusio — *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the beginning of knowledge* (1:7), *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the beginning of wisdom* (9:10), *the fear of Yahuah (LORD) prolongeth days* (10:27). And the fountain-of-life clause is word-for-word the Torah-clause of *The law of the wise is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death* (13:14): the fear of Yahuah and His law are the SAME fountain, departing the SAME snares of death — the Torah is not the curse but the very fountain of life. The restored witness sings it in one voice: *To fear Yahuah (God) is the beginning of wisdom: and it was created with the faithful in the womb* (Sirach 1:14); *The root of wisdom is to fear Yahuah (God), and the branches thereof are long life* (Sirach 1:20). The fear that begins wisdom is the root whose branches are the long life the fountain gives.

threads.title: The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways
threads.summary_md: The chapter weighs the turning-back heart: *The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: and a good man shall be satisfied from himself* (Proverbs 14:14). To backslide is to be filled again with one's OWN ways — the very seems-right way (14:12) made habitual, the heart turned from Yahuah back to itself. Jeremiah names exactly what backsliding is: *thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God), and that my fear is not in thee* (2:19) — backsliding is forsaking Yahuah, and it carries its own correction; the backslidings themselves reprove the man. The New Testament keeps the warning sharp: *if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world... they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning* (2 Peter 2:20); it had been better never to have known the way *than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them* (2:21); *The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire* (2:22). The backslider in heart turns from the holy commandment and is filled again with his own ways — the dog to its vomit — while the good man, who keeps the way, is satisfied from the fruit of it.

threads.title: The heart knoweth his own bitterness — the inward heart and its joy
threads.summary_md: The chapter turns inward to the heart no one else can enter: *The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy* (Proverbs 14:10); *Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness* (14:13); *A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones* (14:30). The heart carries a grief and a joy no stranger can share, and laughter itself can mask sorrow. Qoheleth teaches the same — *Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better* (Ecclesiastes 7:3); *The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth* (7:4) — the fool's mirth ends in heaviness; the wise heart, in mourning, is made better. The book of Proverbs twins the sound-heart verse: *A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken* (15:13); *A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones* (17:22) — the very *life of the flesh* against the *rottenness of the bones*. And the Formed Son gathers the heart's hidden grief into its true end: *ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy* (John 16:20); *your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you* (John 16:22). The bitterness no stranger can intermeddle with is met, at the last, by the joy no man can take away.

threads.title: The sacrifice of the wicked an abomination — the prayer of the upright his delight
threads.summary_md: The chapter sets acceptable worship squarely on righteousness, framed by twin verses: *The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to Yahuah (LORD): but the prayer of the upright is his delight* (15:8), and *Yahuah (LORD) is far from the wicked: but he heareth the prayer of the righteous* (15:29). This is obedience-above-ritual, NOT anti-sacrifice and NOT antinomian — the offering and the prayer alike are weighed by the heart and walk that bring them. The chapter itself frames the verses: *The way of the wicked is an abomination unto Yahuah (LORD): but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness* (15:9); *The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to Yahuah (LORD): but the words of the pure are pleasant words* (15:26). The same book states the measure twice more — *The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with a wicked mind?* (21:27) — and names the anti-antinomian twin: *He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination* (28:9). The prophets pronounce it over whole nations: *To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me?... I delight not in the blood of bullocks* (Isaiah 1:11); *when ye make many prayers, I will not hear: your hands are full of blood* (Isaiah 1:15); *I hate, I despise your feast days... But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream* (Amos 5:21,24). Samuel sets the principle flat — *to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams* (1 Samuel 15:22) — and David sings it from the inside — *thou desirest not sacrifice... The sacrifices of Elohim (God) are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O Elohim (God), thou wilt not despise* (Psalm 51:16-17). And the New Testament keeps the SAME rule, never abolishing it: *Now we know that Elohim (God) heareth not sinners: but if any man... doeth his will, him he heareth* (John 9:31); *whatsoever we ask, we receive of him, because we keep his commandments* (1 John 3:22). The restored witness states it whole — *He that sacrificeth of a thing wrongfully gotten, his offering is ridiculous; and the gifts of unjust men are not accepted* (Sirach 34:18); *The most High is not pleased with the offerings of the wicked* (34:19); *When one prayeth, and another curses, whose voice will Yahuah (God) hear?* (34:24); *He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough* (35:1). From Torah to prophets to Proverbs to the apostles to the restored witnesses the testimony is one: acceptable worship — sacrifice and prayer alike — flows from a righteous, Torah-keeping heart; the worship of the wicked is abomination.

threads.title: The eyes of Yahuah are in every place — beholding the evil and the good
threads.summary_md: The chapter lifts the eye of Yahuah over the whole earth and into the heart: *The eyes of Yahuah (LORD) are in every place, beholding the evil and the good* (15:3), reaching even *Hell and destruction are before Yahuah (LORD): how much more then the hearts of the children of men?* (15:11). Nothing is hidden — not place, not the grave, not the heart. The same book says it in ch5 — *For the ways of man are before the eyes of Yahuah (LORD), and he pondereth all his goings* (5:21) — and the histories, the wisdom, and the prophets fill it out: *the eyes of Yahuah (LORD) run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him* (2 Chronicles 16:9); *his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings* (Job 34:21); *mine eyes are upon all their ways: they are not hid from my face, neither is their iniquity hid from mine eyes* (Jeremiah 16:17); *Yahuah (LORD) looketh from heaven; he beholdeth all the sons of men* (Psalm 33:13). The New Testament keeps the all-seeing eye whole — *Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do* (Hebrews 4:13) — and presses it to the inward parts with a requital attached: *I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works* (Revelation 2:23). The eyes that behold the evil and the good are not idle; what they see, the hand of Yahuah requites. (Cross-lateral to ch5's eyes-of-Yahuah thread.)

threads.title: The fear of Yahuah the instruction of wisdom — before honour is humility
threads.summary_md: The chapter closes on the book's great motto and its humility-refrain in one verse: *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility* (15:33). The whole chapter's reproof-and-instruction strand resolves here — *A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent* (15:5); *The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise* (15:31); *He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding* (15:32) — for the instruction of wisdom is the fear of Yahuah, and the teachable ear is the humble one. The motto is the book's recurring frame: *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction* (1:7); *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the beginning of wisdom* (9:10). And the humility-half is its own refrain: *Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility* (18:12); *By humility and the fear of Yahuah (LORD) are riches, and honour, and life* (22:4). The New Testament carries the humility-before-honour whole — *Elohim (God) resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble* (James 4:6); *Humble yourselves in the sight of Yahuah (Lord), and he shall lift you up* (James 4:10); *be clothed with humility: for Elohim (God) resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble* (1 Peter 5:5); *Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of Elohim (God), that he may exalt you in due time* (1 Peter 5:6). The restored witness keeps the fear-half — *To fear Yahuah (God) is the beginning of wisdom* (Sirach 1:14). The way to honour runs down through humility; the way to wisdom runs through the fear of Yahuah. (Cross-lateral to the fear-of-Yahuah motto threads.)

threads.title: A soft answer, a wholesome tongue — a tree of life
threads.summary_md: The chapter opens on the tongue and returns to it again and again: *A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger* (15:1); *The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness* (15:2); *A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit* (15:4); *A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!* (15:23); *The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things* (15:28). The same book elsewhere weighs the tongue: *A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver* (25:11); *By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone* (25:15) — the gentle word does what the harsh word cannot. The tree-of-life figure of the wholesome tongue reaches back to Wisdom and to Eden: *She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her* (Proverbs 3:18); *the tree of life also in the midst of the garden* (Genesis 2:9). The New Testament keeps the tongue's measure whole: *Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man* (Colossians 4:6); *Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers* (Ephesians 4:29); *let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath* (James 1:19), *For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of Elohim (God)* (1:20). The wholesome tongue gives life and turns away wrath; the perverse tongue is a breach in the spirit.

threads.title: A merry heart hath a continual feast
threads.summary_md: The chapter twins the heart and the countenance through the joy that springs from within: *A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken* (15:13); *All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast* (15:15); *The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart: and a good report maketh the bones fat* (15:30). The same book says it again: *A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones* (17:22) — the glad heart heals, the broken heart wastes. And the source of the feast is named where the Torah was read aloud and the people wept: *neither be ye sorry; for the joy of Yahuah (LORD) is your strength* (Nehemiah 8:10) — the continual feast is no idle mirth but the strength that joy in Yahuah gives. The restored witness roots that joy in the fear of Yahuah itself: *The fear of Yahuah (God) makes a merry heart, and gives joy, and gladness, and a long life* (Sirach 1:12) — binding the merry heart back to the fear-motto that closes the chapter. The cheerful countenance is the overflow of a heart glad in Yahuah.

threads.title: Better is little with the fear of Yahuah
threads.summary_md: The chapter weighs two scales and finds the lesser portion the greater good: *Better is little with the fear of Yahuah (LORD) than great treasure and trouble therewith* (15:16); *Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith* (15:17). What makes the little better is not the littleness but the fear of Yahuah and the love that go with it. The same book repeats the form: *Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right* (16:8); *Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife* (17:1). The Psalter sings the same balance: *A little that a righteous man hath is better than the riches of many wicked* (Psalm 37:16). And the New Testament seals it: *But godliness with contentment is great gain* (1 Timothy 6:6). The fear of Yahuah with a contented little is the true wealth — gain that great treasure carried with trouble, hatred, and strife can never be.

threads.title: A man's heart deviseth his way — but Yahuah directeth his steps
threads.summary_md: The chapter's spine is the sovereignty of Yahuah over man — man proposes, Yahuah disposes. It opens the theme: *The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from Yahuah (LORD)* (16:1); it states it bare at its center: *A man's heart deviseth his way: but Yahuah (LORD) directeth his steps* (16:9); and it seals it at the close, down to the cast lot: *The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of Yahuah (LORD)* (16:33). This is no fatalism but the Father's rule over the steps of the one who walks. Jeremiah confesses it as a prayer: *O Yahuah (LORD), I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps* (10:23). The same book of Proverbs says it twice more: *There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of Yahuah (LORD), that shall stand* (19:21); *Man's goings are of Yahuah (LORD); how can a man then understand his own way?* (20:24). And David sings the comfort hidden in it: *The steps of a good man are ordered by Yahuah (LORD): and he delighteth in his way* (Psalm 37:23) — the directing is not a cold decree but a delight. The chapter gives man his part too: *Commit thy works unto Yahuah (LORD), and thy thoughts shall be established* (16:3); and even the enemy's peace is His doing — *When a man's ways please Yahuah (LORD), he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him* (16:7), as Abimelech confessed to Isaac, *We saw certainly that Yahuah (LORD) was with thee... they departed from him in peace* (Genesis 26:28-31). The New Testament never abolishes this rule but presses it: *ye ought to say, If Yahuah (Lord) will, we shall live, and do this, or that* (James 4:15); *it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of Elohim (God) that sheweth mercy* (Romans 9:16); *it is Elohim (God) which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure* (Philippians 2:13). Even the very lot of 16:33 falls as He disposes — *the lot fell upon Matthias* (Acts 1:26). The restored witness frames it with the potter: *As the clay is in the potter's hand, to fashion it at his pleasure: so man is in the hand of him that made him* (Sirach 33:13), and counsels the only safe response — *pray to the Most High, that he will direct your way in truth* (Sirach 37:15). From Torah-history to the prophets to the psalmist to the apostles to the restored witnesses, the testimony is one: man may devise, but the Father is sovereign over the heart, the tongue, the steps, and the lot.

threads.title: Yahuah hath made all things for himself
threads.summary_md: *Yahuah (LORD) hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil* (16:4). All things, the wicked included, serve His purpose — not that He authors the evil, but that nothing escapes His ends. Isaiah binds creation to His glory: *Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him* (43:7). Paul gathers all things to Him in one line — *For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen* (Romans 11:36) — and names the Formed Son the agent and the goal: *For by him were all things created... all things were created by him, and for him* (Colossians 1:16); the Word drawn from the Formless is the One through whom the Father made all, and toward whom all is made. Even the hard clause stands: *the wicked for the day of evil* is Paul's *the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction* (Romans 9:22) — no rebel escapes His ends, and His power is made known even in the day of evil. And heaven sings the whole of it: *thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created* (Revelation 4:11). The for-himself of the proverb is the to-him of the doxology and the for-thy-pleasure of the throne-room: all that is, is His, and for His delight.

threads.title: By mercy and truth iniquity is purged
threads.summary_md: *By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of Yahuah (LORD) men depart from evil* (16:6). The two — mercy and truth — are bound together through the canon: *Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart* (Proverbs 3:3); *Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other* (Psalm 85:10); and Micah gathers the whole walk into them — *what doth Yahuah (LORD) require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy Elohim (God)?* (6:8). In the Formed Son the pair takes flesh: *the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us... full of grace and truth* (John 1:14); *the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Yahusha HaMashiach (Jesus Christ)* (John 1:17) — which does not unseat the Torah given by Moses, but names the One in whom the iniquity-purging mercy and truth come to the people. And the purging itself is consummated in the blood: *the blood of Messiah (Christ), who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to Elohim (God), purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living Elohim (God)* (Hebrews 9:14). The restored witness sets mercy and the departing-from-evil beside the purging: *alms makes an atonement for sins* (Sirach 3:30); *to depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to Yahuah (God); and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation* (Sirach 35:3). The second half of the proverb is its own road home — *by the fear of Yahuah (LORD) men depart from evil* — and the highway of the upright is the same: *to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul* (16:17).

threads.title: There is a way that seemeth right — but the end is death
threads.summary_md: *There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death* (16:25) — the verbatim twin of 14:12, doubled in the book for its weight. The way that looks right twice over still ends in death, and the seeming is no guide. The seeming-right is the unweighed eye, which the chapter has already exposed: *All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but Yahuah (LORD) weigheth the spirits* (16:2), restated almost word for word at *Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but Yahuah (LORD) pondereth the hearts* (21:2). It is the fool's error — *The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise* (12:15). Yahusha (Jesus) names the two roads the proverb sets side by side: *wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat* (Matthew 7:13) — the broad road is the one that seems right to the many. And Paul names the wage waiting at the end: *the wages of sin is death; but the gift of Elohim (God) is eternal life through Yahusha HaMashiach (Jesus Christ) our Lord* (Romans 6:23). The way that seemed right pays death at its end; over against it stands the only other way, the gift of life. (Parallel two-ways threads run in ch12 and ch14; this one is sourced fresh from 16:25 and bound to the self-justified eye of 16:2.)

threads.title: Pride goeth before destruction
threads.summary_md: *Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall* (16:18) — the chapter's famous warning, framed by *Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to Yahuah (LORD): though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished* (16:5) and answered by *Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud* (16:19). The same book sounds the sequence again and again: *When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom* (11:2); *Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility* (18:12); *A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit* (29:23). The archetype is the fall behind all falls: *I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of Elohim (God)... Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit* (Isaiah 14:13-15); *Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty... I will cast thee to the ground* (Ezekiel 28:17). And it is made flesh in a king brought low and restored, who confessed it from the far side: *those that walk in pride he is able to abase* (Daniel 4:37). The New Testament keeps the rule unbroken, twice setting down the same standing word: *Elohim (God) resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble* (1 Peter 5:5); *Elohim (God) resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble* (James 4:6); and Yahusha states the exchange plain — *whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted* (Luke 14:11). The restored witness traces the root: *Pride is hateful before Yahuah (God) and man* (Sirach 10:7); *The beginning of pride is when one departs from Yahuah (God), and his heart is turned away from his Maker* (10:12); *pride is the beginning of sin... and therefore Yahuah (God)... overthrew them utterly* (10:13). The haughty spirit is first a turned-away heart; the fall follows the turning.

threads.title: A just weight and balance are Yahuah's
threads.summary_md: *A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work* (16:11). The honest scale is not commerce alone but covenant — it is the Torah's own command, spoken by Yahuah in His own Name: *Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am Yahuah Elohaychem (the LORD your God), which brought you out of the land of Egypt* (Leviticus 19:36). The bag of the proverb is the very bag the Torah inspects: *Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small* (Deuteronomy 25:13), and the honest weight carries a covenant blessing — *thou shalt have a perfect and just weight... that thy days may be lengthened in the land which Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) giveth thee* (25:15). The same book of Proverbs states it from its underside: *A false balance is abomination to Yahuah (LORD): but a just weight is his delight* (11:1). Because all the weights of the bag are His work, the false balance is His abomination and the just weight His delight — the marketplace measure bound straight to the heart of the covenant.

threads.title: The hoary head a crown of glory — and the ruling of the spirit
threads.summary_md: Near the chapter's close stand two couplets on the dignity of a well-lived, self-governed life: *The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness* (16:31), and *He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city* (16:32). The honour of the aged is the Torah's own command, bound to the fear of Yahuah: *Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy Elohim (God): I am Yahuah (LORD)* (Leviticus 19:32) — and the same book of Proverbs names the crown, *the beauty of old men is the gray head* (20:29). The gray head is no shame but a glory, when it is found in the way of righteousness. The second couplet exalts the conquest of one's own spirit above the conquest of cities: the same book praises it — *The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression* (19:11) — and Qoheleth counsels it: *Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools* (Ecclesiastes 7:9). The New Testament keeps the rule whole: *let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath* (James 1:19). The mightiest victory the chapter names is not over a walled city but over the self — the slow-to-anger man who rules his own spirit.

threads.title: The fining pot for silver — but Yahuah trieth the hearts
threads.summary_md: The chapter turns to the inner man and the One who proves it: *The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but Yahuah (LORD) trieth the hearts* (Proverbs 17:3). As metal is proved in the fire, so the heart is proved by Yahuah Himself — and the same book says it twice more: *Yahuah (LORD) weigheth the spirits* (16:2); *Yahuah (LORD) pondereth the hearts* (21:2). The man whose ways are clean in his own eyes cannot try himself; only Yahuah can. David, far from dreading the furnace, asks for it: *Examine me, O Yahuah (LORD), and prove me; try my reins and my heart* (Psalm 26:2). Jeremiah states it as Yahuah's declared office: *I Yahuah (LORD) search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways* (17:10). And the figure runs forward to the Formed Son: He comes *like a refiner's fire* (Malachi 3:2), to *sit as a refiner and purifier of silver... and purge them as gold and silver* (3:3); the covenant remnant is brought through — *I will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried... It is my people* (Zechariah 13:9). The NT keeps the furnace whole and names its purpose: *the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Yahusha HaMashiach (Jesus Christ)* (1 Peter 1:7); *the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is* (1 Corinthians 3:13). The risen Messiah claims the heart-trying as His own: *I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts* (Revelation 2:23). The restored witness binds the figure tight: *gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity* (Sirach 2:5). From Proverbs to the prophets to the apostles, the trying is not destruction but refining — Yahuah proves the heart to bring the true gold through.

threads.title: Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker
threads.summary_md: The proverb joins the poor man to Yahuah so tightly that what is done to him is done to his Maker: *Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished* (Proverbs 17:5) — the verbatim near-twin of *He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor* (14:31). The ground is creation itself: *The rich and poor meet together: Yahuah (LORD) is the maker of them all* (22:2); *So Elohim (God) created man in his own image, in the image of Elohim (God) created he him* (Genesis 1:27). Job knew it toward his own servants: *Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?* (31:15). Because the poor man bears the image of his Maker, mercy to him is a loan to Yahuah — *He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto Yahuah (LORD)* (19:17) — and mockery of him is reproach to Yahuah. The Formed Son seals it: *Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me* (Matthew 25:40), and its withholding — *Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me* (25:45). Yaakov rebukes the very mockery: *ye have despised the poor* (2:6), whom *Elohim (God) chosen... rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom* (2:5). The restored witness charges the same care: *defraud not the poor of his living, and make not the needy eyes to wait long* (Sirach 4:1). To mock the poor is to reproach Yahuah; to be glad at his calamity shall not go unpunished.

threads.title: He that covereth a transgression seeketh love
threads.summary_md: The proverb weighs two ways of handling a brother's fault: *He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends* (Proverbs 17:9). The same book states the principle plain: *Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins* (10:12). To cover a transgression — not to conceal wrong, but to refuse to broadcast and repeat it — is the work of love; to rehearse the matter again and again is the work of hatred that divides even close friends. The NT carries the covering forward whole: *above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins* (1 Peter 4:8); and James names the restoring it works — *he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins* (5:20). This covering is the very opposite of the man who hides his OWN sin and shall not prosper (28:13); here it is the love that covers a brother's fault and seeks his restoration rather than his exposure.

threads.title: He that justifieth the wicked — an abomination to Yahuah
threads.summary_md: The proverb pronounces a double abomination on perverted justice: *He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to Yahuah (LORD)* (Proverbs 17:15). This is the Torah's own court-standard, stated and inverted: *Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked* (Exodus 23:7); the judges shall *justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked* (Deuteronomy 25:1). To do the reverse — acquit the guilty, condemn the innocent — overturns the very order Yahuah laid. Isaiah pronounces the woe — *Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!* (5:23) — and the same book the curse — *He that saith unto the wicked, Thou art righteous; him shall the people curse* (24:24). This proverb must be read carefully against the gospel: when Yahuah *justifieth the ungodly* (Romans 4:5), He does NOT do what the corrupt judge does — declare the wicked righteous while they remain in their wickedness. The bribed judge calls evil good; Yahuah MAKES the ungodly righteous, satisfying justice through atonement and the repentant faith that turns from the wickedness. The proverb's condemnation of corrupt judgment and the gospel's justification do not collide — both stand: Yahuah does not pervert justice, He fulfils it.

threads.title: A friend loveth at all times — a brother born for adversity
threads.summary_md: The proverb names the friendship that holds when everything else gives way: *A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity* (Proverbs 17:17). The same book knows this friend who outlasts even kin — *there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother* (18:24) — and Ruth lives it in her bitterest hour: *Intreat me not to leave thee... for whither thou goest, I will go... thy people shall be my people, and thy Elohim (God) my Elohim (God)* (1:16). The Formed Son crowns the figure: *Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends* (John 15:13) — the love that loves at all times is the love that lays down its life. The restored witness treasures the same friend: *A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that has found such an one has found a treasure* (Sirach 6:14); *A faithful friend is the medicine of life; and they that fear Yahuah (God) shall find him* (6:16). The brother born for adversity is the faithful friend who fears Yahuah — a defence, a treasure, and the very medicine of life.

threads.title: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine — and the wise restrained tongue
threads.summary_md: The proverb knows the body and the spirit are bound together: *A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones* (Proverbs 17:22). The same book twins it — *A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken* (15:13); *he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast* (15:15) — and Nehemiah names the source of the healing gladness: *neither be ye sorry; for the joy of Yahuah (LORD) is your strength* (8:10). The merry heart that does good like a medicine is not idle mirth but joy in Yahuah, strength against the broken spirit. The chapter closes on the wise, restrained tongue that the same glad-hearted wisdom keeps: *He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit* (17:27); *Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding* (17:28). The book teaches it elsewhere — *In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise* (10:19) — and so does Yaakov: *let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath* (James 1:19). The fool is unmasked the moment he opens his mouth — *a fool's voice is known by multitude of words* (Ecclesiastes 5:3) — and the restored witness states the close outright: *There is one that keepeth silence, and is found wise* (Sirach 20:5). The merry heart heals; the kept silence is counted wisdom.

threads.title: Cause his face to shine upon us — the Aaronic blessing prayed by the people
threads.summary_md: The psalm opens by praying the priestly benediction over the whole congregation: *Elohim (God) be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us; Selah* (Psalm 67:1). These are the words Yahuah put in the mouth of Aaron and his sons: *On this wise ye shall bless the children of Yashar'el (Israel)... Yahuah (LORD) bless thee, and keep thee: Yahuah (LORD) make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: Yahuah (LORD) lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace* (Numbers 6:23-26). And the Torah seals it as Yahuah's own act, not a mere ritual formula: *And they shall put my name upon the children of Yashar'el (Israel); and I will bless them* (Numbers 6:27). The Name is laid upon the covenant people, and He Himself is the One who blesses. The blessing the congregation prays back is the very blessing the priests are commanded to speak — the Torah liturgy alive in the psalter, not abolished.

threads.title: Thy saving health among all nations — the seed-promise: the nations praise WITH his people
threads.summary_md: The blessing on Yashar'el (Israel) turns outward into the saving of the nations — the missionary heart of the psalm: *That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations. Let the people praise thee, O Elohim (God); let all the people praise thee. O let the nations be glad and sing for joy: for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth* (Psalm 67:2-4). This is the Abrahamic promise unfolding. The blessing reaches the nations THROUGH the seed, never around it: *in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed* (Genesis 12:3); *in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice* (Genesis 22:18). Isaiah names the servant who carries it — and notice the order: *to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Yashar'el (Israel): I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth* (Isaiah 49:6) — the restoration of the houses and the light to the nations are ONE work. Paul takes the servant-word as his commission (*I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles... unto the ends of the earth*, Acts 13:47) and then stacks a catena that names the frame exactly: *that the Gentiles might glorify Elohim (God) for his mercy* (Romans 15:9); *Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people* (Romans 15:10); *Praise Yahuah (Lord), all ye Gentiles; and laud him, all ye people* (Romans 15:11). The nations praise WITH his people, not instead of them — for Yahuah has not cast away his people (Romans 11:1-2). The restored Tobit sings the same ingathering: *Many nations shall come from far to the name of Yahuah (God) with gifts in their hands... all generations shall praise you with great joy* (Tobit 13:11). The nations are gathered TO the Name, alongside Yashar'el, never displacing her.

threads.title: Then shall the earth yield her increase — the blessing of the land
threads.summary_md: *Then shall the earth yield her increase; and Elohim (God), even our own Elohim (God), shall bless us* (Psalm 67:6). The psalm prays the Torah land-blessing — the harvest that follows the walk in Yahuah's statutes: *If ye walk in my statutes, and keep my commandments, and do them; Then I will give you rain in due season, and the land shall yield her increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit* (Leviticus 26:3-4). The yielding earth is the seal of the covenant kept, not an accident of weather. The neighbouring psalm renews the very promise: *Yahuah (LORD) shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase* (Psalm 85:12). The blessing on the land is the blessing of Yahuah upon His obedient people — and in this psalm it becomes the sign read by all the ends of the earth.

threads.title: All the ends of the earth shall fear him — the ingathering of the scattered
threads.summary_md: The psalm closes with the farthest reach of the blessing: *Elohim (God) shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him* (Psalm 67:7). The psalter elsewhere sees the same end — *All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto Yahuah (LORD): and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee* (Psalm 22:27) — and Isaiah issues the very call the psalm foresees answered: *Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am Elohim (God), and there is none else* (Isaiah 45:22). The restored Tobit binds this ends-of-earth fear to the two-house ingathering: *he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he has scattered us* (Tobit 13:5). As Yahuah gathers His scattered people home out of all the nations, the ends of the earth themselves come to fear Him — the dispersion regathered and the nations turning, one harvest.

threads.title: Let Elohim arise, let his enemies be scattered — the ark-setting-out cry
threads.summary_md: The great processional opens with the cry of the ark: *Let Elohim (God) arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him* (Psalm 68:1). These are the very words Moses raised in the wilderness whenever the ark set forward — *And it came to pass, when the ark set forward, that Moses said, Rise up, Yahuah (LORD), and let thine enemies be scattered; and let them that hate thee flee before thee* (Numbers 10:35). The psalm takes up the march-cry of the wilderness and makes it the overture of the whole song: the Formed Son who went before the host, who is among His people as in Sinai, rises — and at His rising the enemies are scattered like smoke driven away.

threads.title: Extol him that rideth upon the heavens — the cloud-rider theophany
threads.summary_md: Twice the psalm names the Rider: *Sing unto Elohim (God), sing praises to his name: extol him that rideth upon the heavens by his name JAH* (Psalm 68:4), and *To him that rideth upon the heavens of heavens, which were of old; lo, he doth send out his voice, and that a mighty voice* (68:33). Read through the Formed and the Formless, this Rider is the One who appears, the Formed Son who comes down upon the heavens. Moses' blessing knows Him: *who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky* (Deuteronomy 33:26). David's deliverance-psalm sees Him fly: *he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind* (Psalm 18:10). The creation-psalm makes the clouds His chariot: *who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind* (Psalm 104:3). And Isaiah carries the cloud-rider into judgment: *Behold, Yahuah (LORD) rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt* (Isaiah 19:1). The Rider upon the heavens is Yahuah who has a Father — the One who later comes on the clouds.

threads.title: A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows — Yahuah's care for the helpless
threads.summary_md: The Rider upon the heavens stoops to the helpless: *A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is Elohim (God) in his holy habitation. Elohim (God) setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains* (Psalm 68:5-6). This is no afterthought — it is covenant-instruction from Sinai itself: *He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment* (Deuteronomy 10:18). The psalter doubles the witness: *Yahuah (LORD) preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow* (Psalm 146:9). And James makes the mercy of Yahuah the very measure of true worship: *Pure religion and undefiled before Elohim (God) and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction* (James 1:27). The people who serve the Father of the fatherless do as their Father does — Torah-mercy carried whole into the apostolic word.

threads.title: The earth shook, even Sinai itself — the theophany and the myriads of holy ones
threads.summary_md: The psalm remembers the day of fire: *O Elohim (God), when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst march through the wilderness; Selah: The earth shook, the heavens also dropped at the presence of Elohim (God): even Sinai itself was moved at the presence of Elohim (God), the Elohim (God) of Yashar'el (Israel)* (Psalm 68:7-8), and names the host that attends Him: *The chariots of Elohim (God) are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels: Yahuah (Lord) is among them, as in Sinai, in the holy place* (68:17). Exodus shows the mount on fire: *mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke... and the whole mount quaked greatly* (Exodus 19:18). Deborah sings it almost word for word: *The mountains melted from before Yahuah (LORD), even that Sinai* (Judges 5:5). Moses names the myriads and the fiery law: *he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law for them* (Deuteronomy 33:2). The writer to the Hebrews names the unapproachable mount: *the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire* (Hebrews 12:18), before which even *Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake* (12:21). And the restored Enoch sees the same coming: *the eternal Elohim (God) will tread upon the earth, (even) on Mount Sinai... from the heaven of heavens* (1 Enoch 1:4); *the high mountains shall be shaken... And shall melt like wax before the flame* (1:6, cf. 68:2); *He cometh with ten thousands of His set-apart ones* (1:9). The thousands of angels of the psalm are the heavenly chariotry that attended the giving of the fiery law; Enoch's set-apart ones who come with him are another company — the seed of promise, gathered and coming with him into the land (Zechariah 14:5).

threads.title: Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive — the ascended Son receives gifts to give
threads.summary_md: The keystone of the processional is the ascension itself: *Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men; yea, for the rebellious also, that Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) might dwell among them* (Psalm 68:18). Paul plants this psalm in the ascended Messiah: *Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men* (Ephesians 4:8). Read through the Formed and the Formless, the One who ascended far above all heavens is the One who first descended: *He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things* (Ephesians 4:10). And the gifts received are the gifts distributed to equip the gathered people: *he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers* (Ephesians 4:11). Peter names the same received-to-give at the ascension: *Therefore being by the right hand of Elohim (God) exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit), he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear* (Acts 2:33). The psalm's *thou hast received gifts for men* is the ascended Son receiving of the Father and pouring out upon His people — He is Yahuah and HAS a Father, ascended that Yahuah Elohim might dwell among them.

threads.title: Unto Yahuah belong the issues from death — the keys of the grave
threads.summary_md: The psalm confesses where the power over death lies: *He that is our Elohim (God) is the Elohim (God) of salvation; and unto GOD Yahuah (Lord) belong the issues from death* (Psalm 68:20). The issues from death belong to Yahuah because He alone ransoms from the grave: *I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction* (Hosea 13:14). The psalter answers its own confession: *But Elohim (God) will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. Selah* (Psalm 49:15). And the risen Son holds the very keys the psalm names: *I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death* (Revelation 1:18). The God of salvation is the One who died and is alive for evermore; the issues from death are His to open.

threads.title: Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands — the ingathering of the nations
threads.summary_md: The processional reaches the nations: *Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto Elohim (God). Sing unto Elohim (God), ye kingdoms of the earth; O sing praises unto Yahuah (Lord)* (Psalm 68:31-32). Isaiah names the ingathering — and guards it: *Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Yashar'el (Israel) mine inheritance* (Isaiah 19:25). Egypt is called His people and Assyria the work of His hands, yet Yashar'el remains *mine inheritance*: the nations are joined IN, never a replacement of the covenant people. Zephaniah carries the stretched-out hands of Ethiopia forward: *From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia my suppliants, even the daughter of my dispersed, shall bring mine offering* (Zephaniah 3:10). The companion psalm reckons Egypt and Ethiopia among Zion's citizens: *behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there* (Psalm 87:4). And the firstfruit walks the desert road: *behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians... had come to Jerusalem for to worship* (Acts 8:27) — Ethiopia's hands stretched out unto Elohim in him, going on his way rejoicing.

threads.title: Make haste, O Elohim, to deliver me — the urgent cry, the detached strophe of Psalm 40
threads.summary_md: Psalm 70 opens and closes on a single urgent plea: *Make haste, O Elohim (God), to deliver me; make haste to help me, O Yahuah (LORD)* (Psalm 70:1), and again at the end *make haste unto me, O Elohim (God)... O Yahuah (LORD), make no tarrying* (Psalm 70:5). This is the very strophe that closes Psalm 40, detached and set alone as the bare cry for haste — the parent twin reads *Be pleased, O Yahuah (LORD), to deliver me: O Yahuah (LORD), make haste to help me* (Psalm 40:13). The cry runs through the whole psalter of the afflicted: the suffering psalm of the pierced One pleads *be not thou far from me, O Yahuah (LORD): O my strength, haste thee to help me* (Psalm 22:19); the penitent cries *Make haste to help me, O Yahuah (Lord) my salvation* (Psalm 38:22); and the psalm that follows takes the cry straight on — *O Elohim (God), be not far from me: O my Elohim (God), make haste for my help* (Psalm 71:12). The one who prays is the poor and needy one, begging Yahuah to bow His ear and make no tarrying — *Bow down thine ear, O Yahuah (LORD), hear me: for I am poor and needy* (Psalm 86:1).

threads.title: Let them be ashamed that seek after my soul — the mockers' Aha, aha turned back
threads.summary_md: The prayer asks that the persecutors be put to shame: *Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt. Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha* (Psalm 70:2-3). The parent strophe of Psalm 40 cries the same — *Let them be ashamed and confounded together that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be driven backward and put to shame that wish me evil. Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha* (Psalm 40:14-15). And the same soul-seekers and the same scorner's cry run through Psalm 35 — *Let them be confounded and put to shame that seek after my soul: let them be turned back and brought to confusion that devise my hurt* (Psalm 35:4); *they opened their mouth wide against me, and said, Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it* (Psalm 35:21); *Let them be ashamed and brought to confusion together that rejoice at mine hurt: let them be clothed with shame and dishonour that magnify themselves against me* (Psalm 35:26). The persecutors of the righteous are turned back upon their own shame; the mocking *Aha, aha* recoils on the one who jeered.

threads.title: Let such as love thy salvation rejoice — the seekers' joy and the poor and needy
threads.summary_md: The prayer turns from the enemies to the remnant: *Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let Elohim (God) be magnified* (Psalm 70:4). The parent strophe twin sings it the same — *Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: let such as love thy salvation say continually, Yahuah (LORD) be magnified* (Psalm 40:16): the seekers who love His salvation are the ones whose continual word is that Elohim be magnified. And the one who prays names himself among the lowly — *But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O Elohim (God): thou art my help and my deliverer; O Yahuah (LORD), make no tarrying* (Psalm 70:5) — the closing verse of the parent strophe, the twin: *But I am poor and needy; yet Yahuah (Lord) thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my Elohim (God)* (Psalm 40:17). It is the very self-naming that opens Psalm 86 — *Bow down thine ear, O Yahuah (LORD), hear me: for I am poor and needy* (Psalm 86:1). The lowly who love His salvation are the ones Yahuah hastes to, and upon whom He thinks.

threads.title: In thee do I put my trust; let me never be confounded — the Rock, the stone in Zion
threads.summary_md: The prayer of the aged servant opens with the very words of an earlier psalm: *In thee, O Yahuah (LORD), do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion. Deliver me in thy righteousness* (Psalm 71:1-2); *Be thou my strong habitation... thou art my rock and my fortress* (71:3). It is the twin of *In thee, O Yahuah (LORD), do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed: deliver me in thy righteousness* (Psalm 31:1) — one prayer taken up again at the close of a life. The Rock he makes his fortress is the Formed Son — *that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Messiah (Christ)* (1 Corinthians 10:4); *He is the Rock, his work is perfect* (Deuteronomy 32:4). And the never-confounded trust is the stone laid in Zion: *Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste* (Isaiah 28:16) — quoted by Paul and Peter as the standing promise — *whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed* (Romans 9:33; Romans 10:11); *he that believeth on him shall not be confounded* (1 Peter 2:6). The restored wisdom tests the plea against all the ages — *did ever any trust in Yahuah (God), and was confounded?* (Sirach 2:10). To trust the Rock is never to be put to shame.

threads.title: Thou art my trust from my youth — holden up from the womb to old age
threads.summary_md: *For thou art my hope, O Yahuah (Lord) GOD: thou art my trust from my youth. By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels* (Psalm 71:5-6). The trust is a lifelong carry, and Isaiah sets the twin word — spoken to the two-house people: *Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Yashar'el (Israel), which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb: and even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you* (Isaiah 46:3-4). The very prayer of the psalm — *Cast me not off in the time of old age* (71:9) — is answered there: He who held him from the womb carries him to the gray hairs. David sang it first in the psalm of the cross — *thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts* (Psalm 22:9) — and the trust reaches back even before the womb — *Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee* (Jeremiah 1:5). From the first breath to the last, the same hand bears him.

threads.title: Forsake me not in old age — until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation
threads.summary_md: *Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth* (Psalm 71:9); *Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O Elohim (God), forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come* (71:18). The plea rests on the standing covenant word — *he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee* (Hebrews 13:5). And the grayheaded servant's task is the commanded work of transmission: *We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of Yahuah (LORD), and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done* (Psalm 78:4); *thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way* (Deuteronomy 6:7) — the Torah handed down. The restored wisdom crowns the very man the psalm pictures: *Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of Yahuah (God) is their glory* (Sirach 25:6). The aged are not cast off; their long experience is given to declare His strength to the generation to come.

threads.title: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only
threads.summary_md: *My mouth shall shew forth thy righteousness and thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers thereof. I will go in the strength of Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD): I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only* (Psalm 71:15-16). The boast is not the servant's own righteousness but Yahuah's — His covenant faithfulness, declared and not hidden: *I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation... from the great congregation* (Psalm 40:10). Paul names the same righteousness OF Elohim: *therein is the righteousness of Elohim (God) revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith* (Romans 1:17); *the righteousness of Elohim (God) without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets* (Romans 3:21). It is righteousness apart from flesh-merit — yet *witnessed by the law and the prophets*, never abolishing them; the Torah and the prophets testify the very righteousness the psalmist boasts. Of thine only — His righteousness alone, not the servant's, and not set against the covenant He gave.

threads.title: Thou shalt quicken me again, and bring me up again from the depths of the earth
threads.summary_md: *Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth* (Psalm 71:20). It is the resurrection hope spoken at the edge of the grave — the same raising the psalter testifies as done: *O Yahuah (LORD), thou hast brought up my soul from the grave: thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit* (Psalm 30:3). The prophet sings it of the whole people: *After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight* (Hosea 6:2). And it is fulfilled in the resurrection by the Spirit — *he that raised up Messiah (Christ) from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you* (Romans 8:11); *this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality... Death is swallowed up in victory* (1 Corinthians 15:54). Brought up again from the depths of Sheol, the aged servant is quickened and raised incorruptible.

threads.title: Truly Elohim is good to Yashar'el — even to such as are of a clean heart
threads.summary_md: The great theodicy opens not with a question but with a thesis, and a narrowing: *Truly Elohim (God) is good to Yashar'el (Israel), even to such as are of a clean heart* (Psalm 73:1). The good of Elohim is real, but it is for the clean of heart — and the whole psalm will test that thesis against the prosperity of the wicked before returning to it. The Formed Son spoke the same beatitude on the mount: *Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see Elohim (God)* (Matthew 5:8). And the Psalter had already set the clean heart at the door of the sanctuary itself: *Who shall ascend into the hill of Yahuah (LORD)? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart* (Psalm 24:3-4) — the very sanctuary where, four verses on, Asaph will go in and understand the end of the wicked (73:17). The good is for the clean heart, and the clean heart is the one that may stand in the holy place and see Elohim.

threads.title: My feet were almost gone — I was envious at the prosperity of the wicked
threads.summary_md: Here is the stumbling that nearly cost Asaph his faith: *But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked* (Psalm 73:2-3). He catalogues their ease — *there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm* (73:4) — and confesses the bitter conclusion he nearly drew: *Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency* (73:13). It is the perennial question of the covenant. Job pressed it: *Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power?* (Job 21:7). Jeremiah pleaded it to Yahuah's face: *Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?* (Jeremiah 12:1). And the wisdom of Proverbs names both the snare and its cure: *Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of Yahuah (LORD) all the day long. For surely there is an end* (Proverbs 23:17-18); *Be not thou envious against evil men... For there shall be no reward to the evil man; the candle of the wicked shall be put out* (Proverbs 24:1,20). The envy is answered only by the end — which the next thread will show is seen in the sanctuary.

threads.title: Until I went into the sanctuary of Elohim — then understood I their end
threads.summary_md: This is the hinge of the whole psalm, the turning of the theodicy: *When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me; Until I went into the sanctuary of Elohim (God); then understood I their end* (Psalm 73:16-17). The riddle of the prospering wicked cannot be solved by staring at the prosperity; it is broken in the appointed place of worship, where the latter-end is seen. The neighbouring psalm declares that end: *Mark the perfect man, and behold the upright: for the end of that man is peace. But the transgressors shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off* (Psalm 37:37-38). The proverb names it: *There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death* (Proverbs 14:12).
